If it were necessary to find one single word that would truly characteriz e
the Brother who has se rved as our ! 16th Grand Master of Masons in
California and Hawaii , that word would unquestion ably be ''warmth." So
strong. so sincere, so all-embrac ing has been the natural warmth and outgoing love exemplified by the Most Worshipful Robert 0. West. that none
of the hundreds whose lives he has touched during his term as Grand
Master has failed to feel and respond to its inspiration and encourage ment.
Only the 16th Grand Master to rise to that eminence from a small town,
Bob West's deep appreciati on and enthusiasm for the impact of Masonry
on his own life have been embodied in the theme of his term , ·•Masonry:
A Foundatio n for Man. for Family, and for Country.'' Calling upon his
experienc e as the owner of a lumber manufactu ring firm in the heart of
California 's Mother Lode regio n. with its colorful pioneer history and Gold
Rush flavor. he has often been able to bring us a fresh a nd unique view
of our Masonic capabilitie s and rewards. Vigorous , straight-fo rward, and
direct. his constant challenge to the Brotherho od to continue the building
of the Masonic foundation has always been accompan ied by his own wholehearted belief that Maso nry could and should be greater and stro nger for
the benefit of all.
To that end . Grand Master Bob-for that is how we think of himimplcmen ted his " Masonry Out Front" policy hy successfully achieving an
outstandin g "first" for his Jurisdictio n in the publishing and distributio n of
a newspaper insert that told the Masonic story to non-Masons on the
occasion of Washingto n's 250th Birthday. Included in four million editions
of metropolit an nt;wspap~rs throughou t California and Hawaii , this beautiful presentati on accomplis hed the goal of telling the true story of
Masonry to multitudes who would otherwise have continued to believe
the m yths with which the ignorant and prej udiced have so long attempted
to surround our Craft.
From the introducti on and successful spearhead ing as Deputy Grand
Master of his 1981 Resolution approving the concept and cost of the insert,
to its completio n, production , and disseminat ion in Februa ry of 1982 , our
Gra nd Master's conviction of the insert's potential and his devotion to its
attainmen t never wavered. Reaction, not only within this Jurisdictio n but
reflected by the admiration and approval expressed by those of many other
States, proved him eminently right.
To generate an idea, espouse a cause, and see it through to frui tion has
been a typical mark of Bob West's participati on in the interests and affai rs
of his communi ty-particip ation whose beginnings he attributes to the
inspiration of Masonry. A me mber of the Be nevolent Protective Order of
E lks, America n Legion. Rotary Internatio nal ; El Dorado County Boy
Scouts District Chairman . 1969-72, and holde r of the Boy Scouts Silver
Beaver Award , 1970; President. El Dorado County Chamber of Commerce. 1965 ; Member, Marshall Hospital Board of Directors, 1966-75 .
and President 1967-75; President since '75 of Marshall Hospital Foundation; Director, American Heart Associatio n ; Member. El Dorado County
iii

Juvenile Justice Commission; President. Cold Springs Golf and Country
Club , 1961 - 70; recipient of El Dorado County Outstanding Citizen Award.
1973; and designated one of the ten most influential people of his county
in 1980. Boh West's contrihutions of time, energy. and effort to his community have bee n guided by a sincere desire to do for others and an honest
joy in the doing. But. whatever the work . he has always done it as a
Mason.
Raised in El Dorado Lodge No. 26 on October 28. 1954. the then-28year-old initiate found in Masonry the inspiration that was to become so
fundamental to his life. He became Master of his Lodge in 1959, Master
of Northern California Past Masters Association in 1976, DeMolay Dad
Advisor, 1974-75. and received the Legion of Honor in 1979. He served
on the Grand Lodge Committee on Charters for 14 years. and as Junior
Grand Deacon, 1970-71; elected Junior Grand Warden- 1978, Senior Grand
Warden-1979. Deputy Grand Master-1980, and Grand Master in October, 1981.
His membership in Concordant Bodies includes : Scottish Rite Bodies.
Sacramento. 32 Degree; Ben Ali Temple of the Shrine ; Eastern Star, Fallen
Leaf Chapter; Royal Order of Jesters: Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots:
York Rite Mason ; Order of the Amaranth: and National Sojourners. And
to all of these he has brought his joy in the Brotherhood. the warmth of
his humor and friendliness. and a natural and unaffected simplicity that
has endeared him to all .
Our Grand Master's consideration for others led him to propose and
carry through a Resolution as Deputy Grand Master which made it possible to shorten our Annual Communication to three <lays, thus reducing
the cost of this important event and bringing it within reach of many who
would not otherwise he able to attend. The Communication of 1982 has
proven the wisdom and validity of that action.
As Grand Master, Bob West succeeded in hringing to reality his oftproposed idea of a European tour for Masonic families. Seventeen hundred
people-all Masonicly related-took last summer's Rhine River Trip, benefiting from the "organization tour package'' he was able to arrange through
Grand Lodge sponsorship , and benefiting even more from their Masonic
companionship.
A devoted family man . Bob has carried this strong emphasis on both
the personal and Masonic family throughout his term as Grand Master.
He has kept his wife. Jean , almost constantly beside him during his continuous travels , and together they have radiated their special brand of
warmth and friendliness from one end of California to the other. and
throughout Hawaii. as well.
Born August 10. 1926, at Santa Cruz. California, Bob West started
working in his father's lumber mill in Placerville at the age of 14, learning
the business the hard way. He married the lovely and vivacious Jean in
1947 and they have been blessed with six children , now aged 22 through
34. in whom his pride is boundless.
Undoubtedly his proudest moments as Grand Master came last July
when he raised two of his sons to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason

in an outdoor mountain-top ceremo ny. the first Grand Master to enjoy
such a rare pri vilege, and when he bo th dedicated and laid the Cornersto ne
of his own Masonic Lodge in Placerville .
As Grand Maste r. warmth and humilit y have pervaded his actions and
his words. His abiding faith in the triumph of Masonic ideals has been the
to uchstone of the many accomplishments of his term , the result of a leadership of love. Grand Master Robert 0 . West personifies those 4ualities
of loya lty. affection. and dedication that are the foundation of true Brotherhood . His example will continue to be a constant reminder and inspiration to the Fraternity to which he has given so unstintingly of himself.

ONE HUNDRED THIRTY-THIRD
ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
the State of California commenced its One Hundred Thirty-third Annual
Communicatio n in the California Mason ic Memorial Temple, San Francisco, California, on Monday. October 11. 1982. A.L. 5982, at 9:00 A.M .
Prior to Grand Lodge opening. Grand Organist James C. Myers entertained the assembled Brethren with an organ concert. playing the following
se lections: ''Taccata in D Minor," " Fiat Lux (Let There Be Light) ." " Ravel's Bolero," " Hora Staccatto," " I Dream of Jeannie," and " Beyond the
Sea." Grand Lodge was raised by Coolidge Ahlstrom , Master of El Dorado
Lodge No. 26, and James West and Robert A. West, sons of G rand Master
West , both having been raised on July 17, 1982. The gavels used during
th e Morning Session were presented to the Grand Master by his fa mily at
his Installation in October 1981; by El Dorado Lodge No. 26 at the Cornerstone Ceremon y of their new Temple, the gavel being made by William
Covington , P.M .. Gold Hill Lodge No. 32; Hiram Lodge No. 43, gavel
made by Arthur L. Anderson; the 214th District at a Lake Tahoe Lodge
No. 707 Reception; Orosi Lodge No. 383 at their 75th A nniversary; and
El Centro Lodge No. 384 at their 75th Anniversary. Upon the call of the
roll, the following elected and appointed officers responded:

In vocation
Eternal God. we arc thankful for the rich blessings of Masonic fellowship. We acknowledge that it is through Thy Great Providence that we are
now assembled in this 133rd Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free
and Accepted Masons of California and Hawaii. May harmony of purpose
and unity of spirit dominate all our thoughts and actions.
Rekindle the fire of good will upon the hearthstone of o ur better selves.
Let benevolence , large-heartedness, tolerance. and fellowship have possession of our souls.
By waiting upon Thee. 0 Lord , and by seeking more light and fuller
truth, we shall face the uncertain future with courage and be able to stand
steadfastly on the eternal truths of our Ancient Craft. Amen.

Devotional
Most Worshipful Grand Masrer and Members of rhe Grand Lodge:
Our Holy Bible speaks these words to everyone , but especially to this
convocation of Maso ns meeting in our Grand Lodge session:
Ye are the light of the world. A city that
is set upon a hill cannot be hid. Neither do
men light a candle and put it under a bushel.
but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto
all that are in the house. Let your light so
shine before men that they may see your good
works, and glorify your Father which is in heave n.
During this year of 1982. California Masonry has been allowing its light
to shine. It has been like the city set on a hill which cannot be hid. Our
te mples and meeting halls have been see n by all men. The thousan~s of
members who have labored in these temples - busy with Stated Meetings.
practices. committeework, and social events - have been seen as dedi-

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

7

cated citizens working for a better community, a better country. and a
better world .
The steady light of Masonry shines brilliantly in the lives of the children
in the Masonic Home in Covina and in the lives of the adults at the
Masonic Home in Union City. The world sees and appreciates the charitable work done by our Concordant Bodies, as in the modern miracles
achieved in the Shriners' Hospitals and in the Scottish Rite Aphasia Clinics.
Last February 21st. California Masonry placed its lighted candle upon
a golden candlestick when it published a Sunday newspaper supplement
in recognition of George Washington's 250th Birthday Anniversary. On
that day the people of California and Hawaii saw the Ancien t Craft of
Free and Accepted Masons in a new and cleare r light.
The Grand Master's tour of Europe with many Maso ns and their fa milies
added a new dimension to the range of Masonic light. Good will was given
by this happy group of world trave lers, and good will was received from
the people in those European countries.
Early in this year of traveling. the Grand Lodge family conceived its
role as being ·•Ambassadors for Masonry" throughout California and Hawaii. With this thought as our guide, we brought our candles from under
the bushel and had the joy of placing them upon the candlesticks of fellowship and sociability.
The light which we carry forth into the world must be a bright, sustained ,
brilliant Harne of true Masonry. It must gain attention. attract notice , and
cause people to turn to the brightness. This beacon-light must arouse men
from their dreaminess, from their preoccupation with trivial activities. and
from their unprorytable or damaging pursuits. Robert Louis Stevenson
might very well have been talking about the role of a dedicated M ason
when he defined the function of a poet:
" He ( and we will say, 'The Inspired Mason') must
shake people out of their indifference, and force them
to make some election in this world , instead of sliding dully forward in a dream."
We see on all sides of us people mismanaging their lives. Sometimes this
comes through carelessness. but more often the tragedy comes from bei ng
caught in meaningless activities. People are commonly drifting along aimlessly, when they need to be involved in a vital cause for the betterment
of mankind. The radiance of the Masonic life can and will induce men to
sec the great possibilities of o ur existence and to learn the benefits of
fraternal association.
These no ble and open displays of Masonic ideals and virtues are necessary in this present day. Our stand must be clear, and our principles
unmistakable. The world needs and yearns for the bright ray of hope in
the eternal verities of our Ancient Craft.
There are other ways, howeve r, of letting our light ·shine before men .
We cannot always live upon the hilltop. We cannot always stand up and

shout our beliefs. Most of the time we have to speak through the unuttered
words of our conduct and our attitudes. What we are so often speaks
louder than our words. It was the poet-laureate of England, William
Wordsworth , who spoke of the " best portion of a good man's life'' as " His
little. nameless. unremembered acts of kindness and of love." It is somet!m~s difficult for us to think that the best portion of our years of Masonic
~1fe is found in the "little'' things we <lo. They are ''little,'' however. only
rn the sense that the small acts of kindness and love are natural. normal,
and effortless, but the y are not " little" to the one who receives these
kindnesses. We know it to be true that one little gesture or thought has
completely changed the course of a man's life. The deeds are "nameless"
because they have the ineffable quality of being beyond human words.
And, further. these expressions of kindliness are "unremembered" by the
good man who does them because no praise was asked and no reward was
expected. These acts showed true charity. coming from the heart.
.When .Joh.n Ruskin was well advanced in years, he was sitting near a
wrndow m his home watching a lamplighter. On the distant hill the man
with the torch wou.Id ignite the street lamps one by one. The Ia~plighter
could not. be seen m the darkness, but his progress could be observed as
he went from street to street.
After a few minutes , Ruskin turned to a friend and said that the Iamp~ighter wa~ the per~e~t illustration of what happens as a good man makes
h~s rounds m dally hvrng. "You may not know him , or ever see him , but
~1s way has been marked by the lights he leaves burning." The true Mason
1s best known by the many lights of charity and good will which he leaves
burning to light the way for another traveler on life's journey.
George Eliot brings these lines of encouragement to each of us as we
carry the torch of Masonic light to all within the circle of our daily activity:

His love for His flowers, He saw fit to pluck some of them. and take them
to that garde n above, and transplant them where they can bloom more
beautifully tha n ever before.
It is only human that our hearts at this time are touched with a feeling
of sadness. But our hearts are made glad when we hear the words of the
Psalmist who said, "Weeping may endure for a night. but joy cometh in
the morning." I sometimes wonder if these two words are not one and the
same. A prince dressed in poor clothes came to a poor hovel in a small
village and asked hospitality for the night. The family welcomed him with
open arms . In the morning he cast aside his poor clothes and appeared
before his hosts in the garment of a prince. He was the same person the
night before that he was in the morning, but clothed in a different raiment.
In the eyes of God, sorrow and joy are the same, but clad in a different
raiment. In the Book of Zechariah we read: "I will clothe thee with a
change of raime nts ." The departing of our Brothers has been a casting
aside of their earthly garm ents and having been clothed with the garments
of a prince. The night of our sorrow can be followed by the joy of the
morning.
The dark shadow of death has again made its appearance and saddened
our hearts. But I am reminded of someone who said that the shadow of
death is just the shaded hand of God outstretched caressingly toward our
departed Brethren. The death of our Brothe rs is the reaching of the warm
hand of God to receive and caress, and not the cold hand of a monster
snatching someone from us.
Death. the great leveler of mankind. is never idle. He strikes with the
tedious monotony of a metronome. The grim reaper, with his scythe. has
taken from our midst the largest number of Brethren in the history of this
Grand Lodge . For the five hundred and fifteen Masters , Past Masters and
Wardens . "The brittle thread which bound them to earth has been severed,
and the i~ liberated spirits have winged their flight to the unknown world."
Included in this overwhelming number are Committeemen. Inspectors and
the Grand Bible Bearer.
Your Committee wishes it might include in this report even a brief statement of the accomplishments of these dedicated and devoted Brethren
who have so freely and unselfishly given of their time to promote that
spirit of amity and good will which characterizes a Mason . Each, however.
has had a fitting and touching eulogy given by their respective Lodges. w_e
regret that time does not permit the reading of their names; however. their
individual names and Lodges will be inscribed in the printed record of our
Annual Communication.
Of the five hundred fifteen members who have gone to their reward
during the past year, three hundred and sixteen Lodges suffere~ losses.
One Lodge lost nine, two Lodges lost seven each , one Lodge lost six, three
Lodges lost five each , three Lodges lost four each , 30 Lodges lost three
each , 93 Lodges lost 2 each, and one hundred eighty-three Jost one each.
Reflecting on the lyrics of our Memorial Service let us symbolically enact
its message by rising: .. now clasp the hands with the Brothers on either

Every soul that touches yours
Be it the slightest contact
Gets therefrom some good ;
Some little grace ; one kindly thought ;
One aspiration yet unfelt:
One bit of courage
For the darkening sky;
One gleam of faith
To brave the thicke ning ills of life ;
One glimpse of brighter skies
Beyond the gathering mists
To ma ke this life worthwhile
And heaven a surer heritage.

RAYMOND E. WATSON
STATE DEPUTY, KNIGHTS OF COLUMBUS*

At the invitation previously extended by the Grand Master. Mr. Raymond E . Watson. State De puty of the Knights of Columbus. was escorted
into Grand Lodge and addressed the asse mbled Brethren . In his remarks
he stated that many of the principles of our two Fraternities were identical.
commenting that the foremost of these is a belief in a Supreme Being.
Both organizations share the same problems, and we are both striving for
the same basic goals. He concluded his remarks hy saying that there is a
definite need in the world today for the ideals of fratemalism, and he
invited the Grand Master, or his representative , to attend the Knights of
Columbus Convention, to be held in Redding during the month of May,
1983. His remarks were accorded a standing ovation as he was escorted
from the Grand Lodge.

Masons Abroad
Another highlight of my year as Grand Master, though of a very differen t kind. was the tremendously successful Rhine Country Tour that took
place this past summer. For a number of yea rs I had had the idea that
Masons should be able to tour as a group. and , thanks to receiving Grand
Lodge approval last Fall , we were able to put this idea into practice. But
even l had no idea the trip we planned would be so popular! We had 1.700
people, Masons and their families throughout California who took advantage of o ur program . Twelve groups left from San Francisco and sixteen
groups left from Los Angeles, 40 to 120 in a group.
We traveled 2,300 well-planned miles through Europe--Holland. Belgium. Germany. Switzerland , and Austria. We cruised down the Rhine
River. visited castles and cathedrals where we could see on the blocks of
stone the individual marks of the Masons who had built them. We visited
the home of the great composer Mozart. and had dinner with the Grand
Master of the American-Canadian Grand Lodge of Germany, and seven
of his Grand Lodge officers.
There were a good many o lder people who took the trip-one in our
party was 89--who said they were able to realize this long-cherished dream
be~au se th_ey felt s~fe traveling with Masonic families rathe r than st rangers.
This security of being toget her with some of their own in a strange country
ga_v e many the feel.ing of confidence the_y needed to make the trip. something they wouldn t have done o therwise . Hundreds of new friendships
were made due to this opportunity for Fraternal interchange. and I a m
c?nvinced that the exchange of Masonic enthusiasm among membe rs from
different areas has a most healthy effect on the Craft and should be continued.
T~e trip \Vas_ an excellent ''buy" and a gre at savings to our members.
But 1t had a sptn-off benefit. in that the money for the tickets pre-paid by
our '!1em?ers earned some $11.473.(X) in interest for Grand Lodge during
the time 1t was on deposit. This money will be presented to the California
Masonic Foundation to assist in providing scholarships for the benefit of
mankind. and for the further enhancement of o ur Fraternity's image.

A Media Event
Thanks also to Grand Lodge approval last Fall, an outstanding highlight
of my year as Grand Master was the successful production of the Masonic
newspaper insert which was distributed last February commemorating t he
250th anniversary of George Washington's birthdate. This , too, had been
a long time dream of minc-----communicating with non-Masons on a large
scale as to what Masonry is all about. This was undoubtedly the most
successful and long-lasting effort of my year, which reached four millio n
homes in California and Hawaii with the truth of what we stand for and
correcting many of the misunderstandings and misconeeptions about Freemasonry which have plagued us for so long.
When I presented the Resolution for the special insert last Fall. I made
th_rce promises: I promised the Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that the supplement would be accomplished in good taste; that it would
be financed wholly by Grand Lodge; and I promised th e Finance Committee that the cost would not exceed $1.25 one-time only per capita charge.
As it turned out , the project was paid for by th e Brethren of California
and Hawaii without any outside help. at a cost of $1.13 per capita-12
cents under the estimate.
The net cost was less than anticipated , due to the generosity of a deceased Brother who had donated a substantial sum of money "for the good
of the Order," and which was used to defray part of the expense of t he
publication and distribution.
Beautifully written and edited by Brother Ralph Head . Editor of o ur
California Freemason Magazine. the insert has received congratul ations
and enthusiastic approval fro m Grand Lodges throughout the United States,
so me of whom hope to emulate our example. Thanks to Brother Head's
expertise in telling our Masonic story in such good taste and within t he
confines of Masonic tradition, Lodges in California and Hawaii are feelin g
the impact in increased applications for membership. In the continued
building of the Masonic foundation . the insert has served as an important
keystone.

Grand Masters Conference-Washington, D. C.
In February your Grand Master. accompanied by Deputy Grand Master,
Right Worshipful Harry Maynard, and Grand Secretary. Very Worshipful
Robert A. Klinger, traveled to Washington , D.C. for the Grand Masters
and Grand Secretaries Conference of North America. The Masonic fellowship and exchange of ideas are most helpful from the standpoint of
fraternal relationships. However, it has been the concensus of most of
those attending that the formal meetings are not productive and do not
always justify the expense.
In an effort to increase the effectiveness of the Conference. a committee
was appointed last year to study the entire structure of the Conference
and recommend changes that would make it worthwhile and productive.
This committee, consisting of the Past Grand Masters of Utah , Florida.
Oklahoma, Pennsylvania. and our own Past Grand Master of California ,
H. Douglas Lemons, worked hard and long to develop proposals and
changes , including moving the site of the Conference to some of the Western states, rather than keeping it continually in Washington. D.C.
I am sorry to report that the labors of that committee went for naught;
voting on their recommendations was tabled until next year.
When the Executive Secretary completely ignored the special committee
report and the request for a Conference-site change to one of the Western
States, I strongly objected. After some heated discussion, Texas was approved as the site for the 1983 Grand Masters Conference. and Washington
State for 1984.

Executive Commiuee
In accordance with legislation which was adopted at the last Annual
Communication of this Grand Lodge, I am pleased to report to you that
the Executive Committee has met on a monthly basis. This Committee
comprises the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master and the Senior
and Junior Grand Wardens. The Grand Secretary is present to record all
action items and relate those matters of import which cross his desk.
These Executive Committee meetings are most worthwhile and productive and are of great help to the Grand Master in receiving input as it
relates to problems which must be solved, decisions which must be forthcoming and action which must be taken. In addition , I believe it to be of
immense benefit to the progressive elective officers in their service to the
Craft in the future. Another most important benefit that results from these
meetings is that a continuity of thought and action is developed which can
be of value to the Grand Lodge, particularly in the area of on-going programs.
It has been a wonderful and gratifying experience for me to have worked
so closely with your Deputy and your Grand Wardens this past year. Much

DEC ISION
I was asked about the status of one who had submitted an application
for the degrees of Masonry to Lodge " A" and had been objected to. The
objection was not withdrawn within the 60 day period as provided by law,
and the applicant therefo re stood rej ected . No written notice of th is rejection was sent to th e applicant. Instead, he was informed verbally by the
Secretary. who called at his residence to return his fees and contributions
that his application was ~or acted upon . In a period of time less than th~
required 12 months. the applicant applied to Lodge '' B" for the degrees
of Masonry. answering affirma tively to the question on the application.
" Have you ever prese nted an application to any Maso nic Lodge?'' In response to the question, " If so, when and to what Lodge o r Lodges?", the
applicant answered "Lodge A". In answer to the questio n . " Have you ever
been rejected by any Masonic Lodge?", the applicant answered in the
negative. Since no formal rejection notice was sent to the applicant as
required , but only that he was informed verbally th at his application was
not acted upon, we must assume that he truthfully believed that he had
not been rejected .
It was quite apparent that Lodge "B'' did an extremely poor job of
investigation. and based upon this poor investigation report, Lodge " B''
acted favorably upon the ap plication . Subsequently. this came to the attention of Lodge "A" but not before Lodge " B" had conferred the Entered
Apprentice Degree upo n the applicant. Lodge " B", when so informed that
they had acted illegally in accepting the application in the first instance,
re fused the Candidate advancement and properly refunded to Lodge ''A"
the fee for the sntered Apprentice degree conferred . They also properly
made the appropriate refund to the Candidate.
The question arose as to the status of the applicant, and which Lodge
had jurisdiction over him . I responded by stating that the innocent applicant, although initiated illegally, was properly an E ntered Appre ntice Mason under the jurisdictio n of neither Lodge "A" nor Lodge ''B'' since he
had been rejected by Lodge "A" and had had his fees and contributions
ret urned and had been stopped from advancement by Lodge '' B" and had
had his unearned deg ree fees and contributions returned. Therefore, not
being unde r the j urisdiction of either Lodge the Candidate was at liberty
to apply for the remaining degrees in any recognized Lodge at any time
after the expiration of 12 months from the date of the first degree conferral
by Lodge "B".
RECOMMENDATI ONS

Number /.-District Grand L odge of Hawaii
At the conclusion of the 1981 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge
it was decided that the special Ad-Hoc Committee studying the possibility
of the formation of a Grand Lodge of Hawaii be discharged, their labors
having been faithfully performed and concluded. The Committee was notified of this action by letter on November 3, 1981.

35

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRA ND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The question of forming a Grand Lodge o f Hawaii continues to be
discussed among the Brethren both on the beautiful Islands of th e Aloha
State and on the Mainland. This is particularly so now that Hawaii remains
the only sovereign state within the United States which does not have its
own Grand Lodge. Your Grand Master is cognizant that committees of
this Grand Lodge for many years have undertaken studies to assist our
Brethren in Hawaii in determining their future within or without o ur G rand
Lodge.
Before being discharged, the Ad-Hoc Committee of this Grand Lodge
re ported that the ma jo rity of Brother Masons in Hawaii did no t feel that
they wished to separate from the Grand Lodge of California and form
their own Grand Lodge. The Ad-Hoc Committee joined in this recommendation, believing that in time the Lodges in Hawaii would become
stro ng and vibrant and able to manage entirely their own affairs under the
auspices of their own Grand Lodge, but such time was not yet propitious.
This Grand Maste r has discussed the future of Hawaiian Masonry with
the Brethren in Hawaii. with the Grand Lo dge Elected Line, with our
esteemed Past Gra nd Masters. and with other Brethren well versed in the
problems, and hopefully in the solution attendant to both the psychological
and fraternal aspects of this problem. Your Grand Master has sought and
received extensive assistance from Brethren not onlv within our Grand
Lodge but from other Grand Lodges throughout the ~orld.
We have been advised that a possible solution for the present dilemma
may be found in th e fo rmation of an intermediate type of organization
presently in use by many of the Grand Lodges throughout the world having
subo rdin ate Lodges within their system not geographically attached to the
Grand Lodge in question . The system used is called a District Grand Lodge
~nd envisions a body of officers governing the District Grand Lodge sub1ect to the Jaws and constitutions of the Grand Lodge itself. It is in effect
a subordinate intermediate jurisdiction between the Constituent Lodges
and the Grand Lodge. It gives the opportunity for a degree of auto nomy
by the local grouping of Lodges, without severing itself from the Mothe r
Grand Lodge . If you will, it permits the child to learn to crawl before it
walks o r runs. This system has worked well for such dive rge nt Grand
Jurisdictions as England. Scotland. Ireland. France, Massachusetts. Italy
a nd Germany. among o thers.
Your Grand Master is of the opinion that a Grand Lodge of Hawaii is
an eventuality. We believe that it is important to give the Lodges within
Hawai i the opportunity to rule themselves in so me limited manner. and
at the same time to learn to govern themsel ves in a structure compatible
with their own requirements. which in some cases may differ substantiall y
fro m those on the Mai nland . The ideas of this Grand Master are not set
in concrete. A great deal of study is necessary. A great deal of disc ussion
must ensue, and the wishes of our Brethre n in Hawaii. as we ll as our
concern for them , must be taken into consideration.
I therefore believe that a special committee should be formed , appointed
by o ur incoming Grand Master, to study the feasibility of establishing such

a District Grand Lodge of Hawa ii under the auspices a nd subordinate to
the Grand Lodge of California. I believe that this or some other type of
provincial district o rganization is impo rtant to the growth and develo pmen t
of Free masonry in Hawaii . Accordingly, I submit the following recommendat ion:
That the incoming G rand Master appoint a committee to study the feasibility of forming a District Gra nd Lodge of Hawaii subord inate to and
unde r the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. and that this
committee repo rt its findings and recommendations to th e Grand Lodge
at its next Annual Communicatio n .

34

Number 2-lnstittllion and Coristirution Ceremonies Be Open to th e
Public
My Brethren . it is very necessary that o ur Fraternity, as far as is possible,
involve the public at all of our events. There is no better way to enjoy
good public relations and thus enhance the image of Freemasonry than to
in clude the non-Mason. Toward this end, all o f our Grand Lodge ce remonies have been opened to the public, with th e exce ption of the Institution of New Lodges and the Constitution of Newly Cha rtered Lodges.
These two ceremonies, as well as all others, are printed and availab le fo r
all to read and I see no reason to continue to hold th em in a tiled Lodge
room. A s regards the Institution Ceremony, prior to the newly instituted
Lodge being opened for the transaction of such business properly before
it. the public would be asked to retire. In the case of the Constitution
Ceremony, the public would be admitted afte r Grand Lodge is opened
and called off. ai;id they would then be asked to retire prior to the closing
of Grand Lod ge.
I feel assured that the mechanics of accomplishing this can be left to the
abilities of o ur Ritual Committee to solve and therefo re I submit my seco nd Recommendation:
That two changes be made in the Book of Ceremo nies regard ing the
Institution of New Lodges and the Constitution of Newly Chartered Lodges
to provide that both ceremonies be open to the public.

Number 3-Consolidation Terms to Provide for Use of L owest Number
Each year several consolidations of Lodges take place. The mechanics
to accomplish these consolidations are provided for in the Califo rnia Masonic Code and must be adhered to before any consolidation approval is
give n. Our Code provides that when two or mo re Lodges consolidate, the
Lodge thus formed may hear the name and number of o ne of the Lodges
composing it, or it may bear the name of one and the number of the o ther.
My concern is not with th e name of the Lodge agreed upon under the
terms of the consolidation agreement , but with the numbe r which is chosen
for the Lodge thus formed. I have noticed over the past several years that

36

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFORNI A

m o re and more consolidated Lodges have chosen the higher number rather
than retaining the lower one.
It is important to understand that when Lodges are chartered they arc
given a number in sequence so that the latest Lodge chartered receives
the next number on the Grand Lodge registry; thus the newer the Lodge
the higher the number. and conversely, the older the Lodge. the lower the
number. By agreeing to the use of a higher number in a consolidation , the
history of the older number disappears forever and the history of the
Lodge thus formed can only date from the institution and subsequent
assignment of the higher number. This. my Brethren. is of great concern
to this Grand Master ns it should be to all who have z.n appreciation of
th e history of California Maso nry. What a shame to deliberately discard
and lose forever what might well be many years of significant historical
background of one of our Lodges.
In accord with my deep concern, therefore. I mak e the following Recommendation:
That Section 2104 of the California Masonic Code be amended to provide that when two or more Lodges agree to consolidate, the Lodge thus
formed may bear the name of any one of the Lodges composing it, but in
no event will it use any number other than the lowest number of the
Lodges so consolidating:

pioneers who crossed the mountains and had faith in the future. So th ese
are the things I have talked about this year. likening them to the love and
faith and courage of our Masonry, and I can only hope that these simple.
basic messages have painted for some of you a differently colored picture
of our Masonic way of life and its values--the kind of inspirational picture
I see from where I stand in the Sierra foothill s.
I ca nnot close this message without expressing again my thanks and
pride in the Grand Lodge Officers who have served with me so faithfully.
Five of these fine Masons were Coroneted this year with the 33rd Degree
of the Scottish Rite~
It was a gre a t loss to all of us and a personal sadness for me and my
Grand Lodge Officers when my Grand Bible Bearer. Brother Kermit L.
McC ull o ugh , passed away last June. Appointed by me to that high office,
Brother Kermit was a religious ma n and a devoted Maso n who bore the
Holy Book in our processions with true dignity and reverence.
Nor can I fail to say a very special thank you to our Grand Secretary.
Brother Robert A. Klinger. for his tireless efforts and the trul y magnificent
job he has performed. Brother Klinger and his staff have d o ne everything
possible to assist me. to support my work, and to lighten my load. Our
association has been a great personal pleasure and I am deeply appreciative.
One person, of course . deserves my appreciation more than any other.
and no amount of thanks could ever express my gratitude for all she has
done for me this year-my very lovely, devoted. patient. often long-suffering but always supportive wife. Jean. Beside me whenever and wherever
I needed her-which was all the time-always faithfully backing me up.
encouraging me. when I faltered. applauding my successes. glossing o ve r
m y failures. keeping step with me through the longest days and most ardu o us nights. the fin est assistant Grand Maste r a Grand Master ever had,
- that's my Jean! She, too, has given me this year-given it with \oveand a lt I can say is , "Thank you , Jean! I needed that!"
Now I have but o ne more thing to say. o ne last suggestion. For several
hundred years we have referred to ourselves as Speculative Masons , differentiating ourselves from those Operative Maso ns who built the pyramids. the castles and cathedrals, who so carefully and cleverly placed the
stones, one atop the other. to create structures that have withstood the
test of time. They were proud of their work. and when it was finished they
considered it a credit to their Craftsmanship and made those individual
identifying marks-like hallmarks-in the stones they had placed.
When I saw those stones with their marks in Europe. I was proud of
those Operative Maso ns who were the forerunners of our Fraternity. and
I thought about the building th at remains for us to do-the building of
o ur Masonic foundation for Man. for Family. and for Country. I suggest
that we Speculative Maso ns must , in a sense, become Operative Masons
again: that we cannot afford to sit back .and admire our Masonr y as some-

Farewell-But Not Goodbye
When I became Junior Grand Warden , there were many in the audience
who thought San Francisco was having another earthquake. We weren't.
It was only my knees knocking that rocked the Temple. I promised then
to give my total commitment to my Masonic labors, and I believe I have
done so. These have been wonderful years. filled with wonderful peo ple,
wonderful friendships. I have enjoyed it all to the fullest. And this past
year as Grand Master has been the greatest of my life-I thank God, and
all of you , for giving it to me.
Last year at this time, I told you there was no place in the world I'd
rather be, no one in the world I'd rather be. I can repeat that now, because.
having experienced this fantastic year that I could never have imagined.
m~ heart and soul have been so enriched I would not exchange myself or
this place for any other. There could be nothing more grand than to have
been your Grand Maste r!
When I became the I 16th Grand Master of this Grand Lodge, I was
only the 16th holder of this office to come from a small town. I was aware
that I fell far short of the sophistication and intellectual background of so
many former Grand Masters. l had only the love of Masonry, some knowledge of trees and timber and people. some familiarity with -the gold of my
Mo ther Lode territory, some feeling for the courage of the California

of our Brotherhood , the Square and Compass of our Faith to guide us in
building straight and true. We need only to don our aprons and get to
work!

DECISION No. l

STATUS OF REJECTED ENTERED APPRENTICE

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which the Grand Master's Decision has been referred. reports as follows:
The Grand Master has properly determined that an applicant who has
been stopped from advancement after receiving the Entered Apprentice
Degree has the status of one rejected for the unconferred degrees and may
apply for advancement after 12 months from the date of the conferral of
the Entered Apprentice Degree as provided in Section 2666 of the California Masonic Code.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the approval of
the Decision.
Since neither the Grand Master's Decision nor this motion amends the
law of the Grand Lodge. only a majority vote is required for adoption.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes commends the Grand
Master for the manne r in which he handled a complicated problem as to
the status of a candidate who had been initiated and later found to have
submitted a defective application unwittingly.
We suggest the approval of the Grand Master's Decision and recommend
a "Yes" vote.
The Grand Master's Decisio n was approved.
RECOMMENDATION No. l

DISTRICT GRAND LODGE OF HAWAII

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Grand Lodge has wrestled for years with the question of the degree
of autonomy to be given to the Lodges and our Brethren in Hawaii.
Previously the question appeared to be whether or not a Grand Lodge
of Hawaii should be established.
Now a new concept has been advanced. Your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes agrees that that new proposal merits study.
We recommend approval of the Grand Master's Recommendation. Approval would be signified by a "Yes" vote.
The Grand Master"s Recommendation was adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee o n Policy and General Purposes believes that it is a
policy of this Grand Lodge to encourage public knowledge of the basic
principles for which it st:rnds and to encourage public attendance at such
portions of our ceremonies as can properly be open to the public. Relatively little: of what we do needs be done in a tiled Lodge room.
The Institution of New Lodges and the Constitution of Newly Chartered
Lodges arc the only Grand Lodge ceremonies not now open to the public.
Even they are in print and are not intended to be secret work. They can
be opened. and we believe the Grand Master's Recommendation to be in
accord with our policies and purposes.
We were concerned as to whether the Grand Master's intent was to
require that the ceremony be a public or open ceremony. With his assurance that he intended that it be optional. that the ceremony may be opened
to the public we recommend approval of the Grand Master's Recommendation No. 2. Approval would be given by a " Yes .. vote.

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Recommendation No. 3 of
the Most Worshipful Grand Master has been referred , reports as follows:
The Grand Master recommends that when two or more Constituent
Lodges consolidate, the consolidated Lodge shall at all events bear the
number of the oldest consolidating Lodge.
To carry out the Grand Master"s intent , your Committee submits the
following legislation:
RESOLVED, that Section 2104 of the California Masonic Code be
amended ~y deleting the 3rd paragraph thereof, and adding in lieu thereof
the followmg: "The Lodge thus formed shall bear the lowest number of
any Lodge thus consolidating. and may bear the name of any one o r mo re
of the Lodges consolidating. The consolidated Lodge, if it hears the name
and number of the lowest numbered Lodge, may retain the Charter and
seal of that Lo~ge, but if it bears the number of that Lodge and another
name. may receive, without charge. a new charter and provide a new seal.
or may have the authorization of such consolidation by the Grand Lodge
endorsed on the churter of the lowest numbered Lodge ."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.

The Committee on Ritual:
As regards this Recommendation by the Grand Master, the Committee
on Ritual was asked by him if there were any reasons why the Grand
Lodge Ceremonies for the Institution of New Lodges and the Constitution
of Newly Chartered Lodges could not be opened to the public.
In researching, it was found that all of the Grand Lodge Ceremonies
with the exception of th ese two are open to the public. Further examination revealed that the re was no material improper to be written and as
such it was felt that no reason existed to bar anyone from witnessing these
ceremonies.
The Institution Cere mony is very similar to a Lodge Installation Ceremony and with the exception of the Lodge opening for the purpose of
adopting its By-Laws at the conclusion of the Institution Ceremony. would
pose no problem other than asking the public to retire previous to the
opening.
The Constitution Ceremony has absolutely nothing other than the instruction page stating "This is a tiled ceremony".
As with all of our ceremonies that include the public. the response from
those present has been overwhelming and can bring nothing but good to
our Order. We feel the Grand Master is very wise in his recommendation
and urge its adoption.
The Grand Master's Re commendation was Adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Ma~te~ reco.m mends th at consolidating Lodges be free to
se lect a name of their choice but must elect to retain the lowest number
of the Lodges consolidating.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee believes that consolidating Lodges should retain the prerogative to negotiate among themselves
both the name and number to be used following consolidation as now
provided by Section 2104, C.M.C.
We heli~ve that the history of Lodges can be retained adequately no
matter which number of the consolidating Lodges is selected.
Your Committee recommends a '"No" vote.
Failing a 516 affirmative vote but receiving a majo rity favorable vote.
the Grand Master's Recommendation No. 3 is held over until the 1983
Communication.

" PUBLIC SCHOOLS:

TEMPLES OF KNOWLEDGE'.

America's publi c schools system was established more than 200 years
ago by our enlightened forefa t he r s who were mind ful that ou r in fant
democracy could not su rvive, no r l ong endure, without the s upport of a n
educated electorate.
In the intervening centuries, t his concep t o f free public educati on
h a s developed into a vast nation-wide system of public schools that c an
be regarded as true Temp l es o f Knowledge.
In these Temples -- our public s chool s -- the c hildren of America
are taug ht the principles of democ racy, the value of liberty and the
benefi ts of freedom .
It i s here that they lea rn of America's greatne ss
and derive inspiration f or its f uture.
In these Temples
our public school s -- the youth of o ur country
receive instruc t i on on h o w to be good citi~ens and become responsible
members o f society.
In these Temples
our public schools -- the young people of our
nation are prep ared to be the leaders of tomorrow -- i n business, in
government , in the arts, and in the professions.
In order to enlist the support of the p ubl ic in maintaining these
Temples of Knowledge at their fu l lest efficiency, thu s to e nrich our
lives and to assure the continuing prominence of America a mong the
nation s of the ~or ld , I do now proclaim
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK during APRIL, 1982
throughout California and Hawaii, and I c all upon a ll Masonic Lodges to
arra nge with the Schools in their area for a mutually acceptable week in
the Month of APRIL to be set as i de for the o bservance o f this event with
appropriate ceremonies a nd programs.
Furthermore, I direct that no Lodge programs or Meetings, other tha n
the Stated Meeting, be held dur ing the designated week which might conflict
with Public Schools Observances; and
That this Proclama tion be read by the Master at the April Stated
Meeting of a ll Lodges and, where feasible~ it also be published i n
Lodge bulle tins or d istributed to each member .

"PROCLAMATION"
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MONTH

PROCLAMATION
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
In the participation of every Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction
in the support of our Masonic Homes in Covina and Union City, every
Master Mason has the opportunity to express his concern for the welfare and care of our children, our widows, and our aged.
Indeed, it
is an opportunity to put into practice the generosity toward the less
fortunate, the benevolence toward those in need, and the charity toward our fellow man which are the ideals of Brotherly love we claim
for our Fraternity.
We are justifiably proud of our Masonic Homes - of the structures
and surroundings themselves, and even more so of the care and consideration and atmosphere to be found within.
No Mason can visit
one of these Homes without experiencing a lift of the heart and a
sense of gratification that he has been able to contribute to the
care of his own.
The joy that giving to this most worthy cause brings to each of
us is the precious . coin in which we are repaid, and repaid a thousandfold.
No other investment bears such interest!
Recognizing that to provide for the maintenance of our Masonic
Homes is the rewarding privilege and welcomed responsibility of every
Master Mason, and an opportunity for loving charity which none would
willingly relinquish, I therefore proclaim the Month of May, 1982 to be
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONTH
and direct this Proclamation to be read by the Master at Stated
Meetings held during the Months of April and May, 1982.
I further
direct that, if convenient, a copy be sent to each member of each
Lodge, so that no Master Mason in this Grand Jurisdiction may be shut
out or denied the opportunity to participate in this worthy service.
Fraternally,

As we look about us in the world today, we must be thankful
for the steadiness of America. What e ver troubles and dissention
we h ave - and we have them, whatever tragedies and political upheavals we have - and we have those, too, the g overnment of the
United States proceeds in an orderly fashion.
Based on a Constitution
that all citizens recognize and accept as the guarantee of their
freedom and the framework of their liberty, the form of our government remains a dependable and known constant. It°lS an intimately
familiar starting point from which each of us may travel forth to
experiment with and entertain new ideas, knowing we can always
return to the safety of the tested structure of our Constitution.
This most successful form of self-government so far designed
by Man is still being pulled and tugged at by citizens who seek to
change or modify the structure in some way, who believe they can
bring the nation closer to the realization of its ideals by adding
to or amending the constitutional framework on which our government
exists. We are constantly exposed to the arguments and pressures
of many groups wanting to make such changes. Some we will consider;
others we will reject.
But we have the right, the freedom, the
liberty to listen and to lend our strength to a cause, without fear.
Our Constitution provides us with all the latitude we need; for this
reason it has endured.
In recognition of the rare and precious benefits we derive from
that most noble document, I proclaim the month of September, 1982,
to be Constitution Observance Month, and direct all consti tu ent
Lod ~ es in Calitornia and Hawaii to participate individually, by
Districts, or by combined Districts in appropriate observances and
meaningful patriotic pro grams to which the public shall be invited.
I further direct that this Proclamation be read at the August
and September Stated Meeting s and, wherever possible, be reprinted
in Lodge Bulletins for September.

Patriotism and love of freedom and individual liberty are not
dead in America; they are alive and well in the hearts of Masons.
Dated: July 22, 1982

their families and friends , living and dead, is stupendous to say th e least.

in your contributio ns to our Endowment Fund, wisely sequestered in reserves by your Homes Board Trustees, adequately ensures the preservation
of our treasured facilities for the care of o ur aged and o ur childre n at

developed .

Last year I reported that the net loss o f members for the year 19801981was4,740. the largest net loss for any year in the histo ry of the Grant!
Lodge of California. This past yea r, for the first time since 1978, o ur net
loss. while still substantial. was less than the prior yea r. It can only be
hoped that this is a trend which will continue and ultimately will result in
a reversal so that gains might exceed losses. I would also point out th at
the number of initiates last year increased slightly over the prior ye ar,
which also may be a trend a nd which will , hopefully. co ntinue.
Slow but steady progress is being made in the inputing of our membe rship dat a for use on o ur in-house computer. It is expected that the complete transition from the use of 3x5 typed ca rds to the use of tlata processing equipment will be accomplished by year's end, after which each
Lodge Secretary will then be furnished with a print-out of the members
o f his Lodge for fi nal correctio ns and updating. In the interim all Lodge
activity as reported each month by the seve ral Lodge Secretaries is being
e ntered directly into our computer system and the use of the 3x5 cards for
this purpose has bee n te rmin ated.

S ECRETA RIES' MANUALS

This past year saw the completion. printing and distribution of a brand
new Lodge Secretaries' Ma nual, replacing the one in use for the past
twe nty years . This new Manual contains many sections no t included in the
former Manual a nd is profusely illustrated with pre-filled sample forms.
which forms are required fo r use by the Lodge Secretary in the performa nce of his office work. It is sincerely hoped that this new Manual will
be of great assistance to all the Secretaries. o ld and new alike. and will
result in less time-co nsuming correspondence a nd its attend ant expenses.
The new Manual should go a long way towa rd enabling the Lodge Secretary to heed the ad monition . .. When in doubt. follow the directions."

TRIAL RECO RD No. 2159

In Trial Record 2159, a member of West Gate Lodge No. 335 was charged
with un-Masonic conduct in that he did commit the crime of Mail Fraud
and did attempt to evade or defeat tax , in violation of Title 18 USC #1341
and 26 U SC #7201.
After a non-response by the accused . th e matter was investigated b y the
Trial Master, who made a finding of Guilty to the un-Masonic conduct and
fixed the penalty at Suspension.
Your Committee on Trial Review believes the acts alleged are of such
se verity that the pe nalty should be raised from Suspension to Expulsion.
We therefore submit the following resolution :
RESOLVED, that the findings of the Trial Master be affirmed but the
penalty be raised to Expulsio n.
TRIAL RECORD N o. 2 180

In Trial Record No. 2180, a Brother of The Ga rdens Lodge No. 621 was
charged with filing ''false a nd fraudulent" income tax returns for the years
1975 and 1976. After trial by Commissio n, he was found guilty of both
specifications and o f un -Masonic conduct, a nd was given the pe nalty of
suspe nsion .
In the U nited States District Court where he had been charged with
similar offenses he had e nte red a plea of guilty and had been placed o n 5
yea rs' probatio n.
The facts indicated that he had been a respected preside nt o f a local
bank , but had been invo lved in "laundering" illicitly obtained m o ni es for
various customers of the bank and that he had profited exceedingly thereby.
(He h ad reported inco me of approximately $260,000 for two years. altho ugh he had received income of over $1.000,000 during that period.)
Yo ur Committee feels that the actions of the accused are of a serious
na ture involving moral turpitude , and made all the more heinous by his
p osition a nd the confidem'e h e enjoyed in the community and his Lodge.
We do no t believe ''the punishment tits the c rime."
We believe th at the pe nalty should be raised to expulsion.
Your Committee therefore submits th e following resolutio n :
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2180. the conviction be affirmed,
but that the penalty be raised to expulsio n.

Your Committee o n Tria l Review considered a n a pplication for Restorati o n by a fo rmer member of Tem escal Lodge No. 314, who was expelled

TR IAL R ECORD N o . 2133

In Trial Re cord No. 2 133, a member o f Elk Grove Lo dge No. 173 was
charged with un-Masonic conduct after having been convicted in the United
States D istrict Court of the crime of conspiring to embezzle a sum exceeding $3,000 from his employer. the United States Pos t Office.
The Trial Master found the accused guilty of the specificatio n and of
un-Masoni c conduct ; h o weve r, he fixed the penalty at re primand in open
Lodge . The ma tte r ca me before your Committee o n Trial Revie w in 1979
at which time it was dete rmined that a reprimand in o pe n Lodge was
wholly inappropriate for the commission of a felony fo r which reason it
reco mme nded to this Grand Lod ge that the penalty be raised to expulsion.
The Resolution to increase th e penalty was adopted .
In August of this year, the former me mber made a pplication to t his
Grand Lo dge for restoration of me mbe rsh ip accompanied by some twentysix lette rs o f endorsement. In additio n, the Maste r and several members
of Elk Grove Lodge personally appeared before your Committee in support of the expelled me m be r and urged that his Application for Restoration he approved .
Altho ugh such showing o f support is given great weight. it is the d uty
of the Trial R eview Committee to seek , as fa r as possible. unifo rmity of
penalty a nd guid elines for restoration of expelled members throughout this
Jurisdictio n .
The commission of a felo ny is a serious crime. This former B rother has
be trayed his e mploye r and even his country as a federal postal employee.
H e has betrayed his family, his community, his Lodge a nd , indeed. all

72

PROCEEDINGS OF TH E

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

Freemasonry. This crime against the moral and civil law should no t be
lightly taken or easily forgiven. The fact that the former member is a hard
worker ; that he has me t his conditions of probatio n ; and that he has apparently rehabilitated himself is, in the opinion of this Committee, insufficient after a period of o nly three years to cause us to recommend to this
Grand Lodge that he be restored to all the rights and privileges of a Master
Mason.
The following resolutio n is the refore submitted:
RESOLVED that the Application fo r R estoration in Trial Record No.
2 133 be denied.

Your Committee finds no fa ult with the procedure, conduct or results
of th e effo rts of the Commission o r Trial Master in finding the guilt of the
accused o r in the pena lty imposed . The Trial Master's written findings,
however, ind icate that the Commission was under the impression that unMasonic conduct in the nature of a felony under civil law mandated the
penalty of expulsion. Such is not necessa rily the case. Because of this. your
Committee believes that the error deprived the Commission o f the discretio n provided by the California Masonic Code to dete rmine the penalt y,
and deprived the accused of due process. Your Committee therefore submits the following resolutio n:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty in Trial Reco rd No. 2178 be
affirmed , but the penalty be set aside and the matter rem anded to the
Lodge for re.imposition of the penalty.

TRIAL RECORD No. 2166
In Trial Review Record No. 2166 a mem ber of Gemini Lodge No. 825
was charged with un-Masonic conduct and plead guilty to a charge of Child
Molestatio n, a violation of the Califo rnia Penal Code, #647-a.
Due to the severity of this charge and the degree of moral invo lvement,
your Committee believes th at suspension is inappropriate and this membe r
must be expe lled.
RESOLV ED, that the verdict of g uilty in Trial Record No. 2166 be
affi rmed a nd the pena lty raised to expulsion .
TRIAL R ECORD No. 2177
Consideration of Trial Record No. 2177 reveals th at " Past Master of
Westminster-Fairvie w Lodge No. 629 was properly charged with un-Masonic conduct. The cha rge followed convictio n in a United States District
Court of the willful filing of a false Federal Income Tax Return and perjury.
There resulted a unanimo us finding by the Trial Commissioners that the
Brother was guilty of the offense alleged. Despite this, the Commissioners.
by a less than unanimous vote, determined that the accused was not guilty
of un-Masonic cond uct.
After a review of the record provided, your Committee has dete rmined
that the nature of the offense of which the accused was fo und guilty clearly
indicates se ri o us un-Masoni c conduct by the accused. and the finding of
not guilty of un-Masonic conduct is a gross violation of Masonic law. Your
Committee therefore submits the fo llowing resolution :
RESOLVED. that th e findings of the Trial Commissioners in Trial Record No. 2177 as to the guilt of the accused o n the specification be affirmed;
tha t the finding of not guilty of un- Masonic conduct be reversed; that the
accused he fo und guilty of un-Maso nic conduct; and that the penalty be
fixed at expu lsion.
TRIAL R ECORD No. 2178
Trial Record No. 2178 relates to a member of U nitcd Lodge No. 374,
charged with un-Maso nic conduct in that he did conspire to and did commit
grand theft. After tria l by Commission. the accused was found guilty of
the charges and a penalty of expulsion was imposed.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Brethren. as I stand at this lectern to deliver my first report. I can't he lp
but wonder if those Grand Lecturers that preceded me, had no t done so
with a great sense of humility and pride, in having been afforde d th e high
honor of serving this great Fraternity. While I cannot speak for th em. I
would like to say that it is a great honor and privilege to serve you in this
capacity.
Another year has carved its niche upon the annals of Freemasonry in
this Jurisdiction. and. in compliance with long established usage. I beg to
submit my report on the labors of the year now past.

placed with the Grand Lecturer in regard to ritual, protocol, and administration. In addition, instruction and exemplification in our r itual were

held on October 3 L 1981 in Fresno; December 5, 1981 in Visa lia and
September 4 and 5, 1982 in Carmel. Ritual Committee meetings were a lso

Ritual ratings of the Officers of our Constituent Lodges - Excellent ,
18% Good. 60% . Fair, 22% . While these ratings are not too bad, improveme nt is needed to increase the "excellent" category and a definite
need to lower the numbers classified as "fair".
The number of Brethren willing to serve as officers is still a very serious
proble m in many o f our Lodges. While some of our Lodges are having no
problem , others are floundering. This is pointed out quite dramatically by
the large number of Past Masters serving in the progressive lines. There
are, presently, well over 460 Past Masters in these lines of progression.
There are also a great number of vacancies listed in many of the Lodges .
Funeral Certificate holders in this Jurisdiction number approximately
1850 or an average of three for every Lodge. The unfortunate part of this
report is that 60 of our Lodges have none, and 84 of our Lodges have only
one. This is an area of deep concern to our Ritual Committee, and one of
our highest priorities in the coming year will be a study of this subject and
some possible recommendatio ns to alleviate the problem.
Your adoption at the 1981 Annual Communication with respect to changes
in the Mortgage Burning Ceremony have taken place and have been used
on at least two occasions. These changes resulted in those in attendance
being able to view the entire ceremony. The ceremony has been greatly
enhanced and its impressiveness has been well received by the general
public .
Candidate coaching is an a rea of concern with this Grand Lecturer. We
are apparently losing members because candidates are not preparing themselves for advancement. While I have no magic formula for improvement
in this regard, perhaps a more aggressive approach to the candidate should
be taken. Coaches should make dates with candidates and follow thro ugh .
I urge the Senior Wardens and Head Candidates Coaches, that are not
already working in this manner, to begin immediately.

Recommendati on No. 2 - We have had several instances in the past

Master, Senior Warden , Junior Warden and Senior Deacon . These Sections of Code are identical except for the officers mentioned previously.
Therefore I shall quote only one, "Section 2514. Qualification of Master.
Before a Master-e lect can be installed there shall be presented to the
Installing Officer the certificate of the Grand Lecturer or of the Inspector
of the District in which his Lodge is situated , certifying that he has personally examined such M aste r-elect and that he is qualified to give the
work and lectures entirely in the three degrees; and that he is thoroughly
proficie nt in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations of the
Grand Lodge which relate to the gove rnment of a Lodge.'' I the refore
recommend that the above Sections of our Code be amended to read, "the
certificate of the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand Lecturer of the
Division in which his Lodge is situated or of the Inspector of the District
in which his Lodge is situated ."

HAWAIIAN MASONRY

In early July, J was privileged to visit our Lodges of Hawaii in the
company of Assistant Grand Lecturer Ulysses G . Patropulos. Due to an
illness in my family, I joined him on the Island of Hawaii, arriving just in
time for the Institution of Kona Lodge. Sch ools of instruction were held
in the Lodges of Kauai, Kilauea and Maui. Moving on to Honolulu , an
all day school was held for the seven Lodges of the Island of Oahu . The
work was exemplified in a most professional manner and the Bre thre n of
those Lodges are to be commended for their interest and eage rness to do
the work properly.
The Lodges of our 50th State are having basically the same problems
that our Mainland Lodges are having - lack of officer material , Past Masters filling stations, lack of petitions for membe rship and too many members that do not reside near their Lodges.
Our Island Inspectors, Bill McKee and Ozzie Lau, are to be commended
for the great work they are doing under the most difficult of circumstances.
These include great distances between Lodges and the fact that they are
unable to attend the many schools of instruction on the Mainland held for
the benefit of the Inspectors.

INSPECTORS

Words alone cannot express the gratitude that should he put forth hy
this Grand Lodge to each and every one of those stalwart performers
known as Inspector. Their diligence to duty and the thousands of hours
put forth for the betterment of our Fraternity should receive only the
highest praise. Were it not for the efforts and dedication of these 163 men.
I would shudder to theorize the catastrophic set backs that might take
place in this Grand Jurisdiction. According to the reports filed with this
Grand Lecturer by the Inspectors of the several Masonic Districts. they
held over one thousand two hundred District schools. That is schools for
multiple Lodges. In addition. over one thousand four hundred schools
were co nducted for individual Lodges. This averages out to about 16 different schools held by each Inspector. 16 nights or days away from their
families in conjunction with their schools for ritual and administration!
Inspectors are expected to be in attendance at the Annual Communication.
In addition, each Inspector attends seminars and must attend schools of
instruction held by the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Grand Lecturer's Annual Conference. These tireless workers sacrifice an untold number
of evenings each year in presenting Golden Veteran Awards on behalf of
our Grand Master. for the presentation of like awards for other Grand
Jurisdictions and for the annual Official Visit in each Lodge in his District.
They devote a great number of their weekends in attendance at Cornerstone ceremonies. other Grand Lodge ceremonies and receptions for the
Grand Master. Many hours of their time are spent in helping Lodges to
prepare for those events just mentioned. They support the Lodges in their
various activities , not only in their own Districts, but also nearby Districts.
They make investigations requested by foreign Grand Jurisdictions and
perform a maze of other Masonic related duties. They represent the Grand
Master in his absence , they aid , advise and assist :in all matters appertaining
to Masonry. These men are the. backbone of this Grand Lodge. They
deserve the highest praise, respect and admiration.
Due to the demands made upon these individuals. turnover in the past
few years has become a problem. The majority of turnover in this past
year has taken place in the over six year category. Contrary to popular
belief, less than 13 % of our Inspectoral Corps have any experience over
10 years. The average term of service, representing the entire corps, is
now only four and one-half years.
It is a pleasure, indeed, to welcome the new Inspectors who have received their appointments this past year, and to those Inspectors who have
chosen retirement , I wish to offer a sincere thank you on hehalf of the
Grand Lodge and myself for the untiring efforts put forth on our behalf
and for the benefit of our Fraternity.

during previous years. formal requests for hudget allocations have been

CRITICISM

You might say that our Fraternity does no t need cntic1sm. To this I
totally agree. However, co nstructive criticism and the recognition that
problems do exist, is the only way that we can overcome them. If we
co ntinue to close our eyes to ohvious facts and continue to paint a heautiful
picture of what is happening within the framewo rk of this Jurisdiction. we
may go the way of the Roman Empire and other fraternal organizations
that are floundering in their own complacent attitudes.
Not many years ago o ur Jurisdiction was riding the crest of a wave. with
our membership well over 240,000. At the beginning of this fiscal year our
m emhership had dropped to 188.535. Brethren, this is a loss of over 25o/c.
In the last two years alone, we have lost over 4600 members annually. It
is time to take a look. It is time to try to analyze just what is happening.
We have a great responsibility as Masons. We tell the world that we
take good men and make them better. Are we really doing this today in
Masonry? How many times have we had the unpleasant experience of
initiating. passing. or raising a Brother and having him go out the door.
never to return? •Too many of our candidates will leave after the First
Degree. Second Degree and even the Third Degree and never come back.
Why? The answer may be obvious and perhaps falls into two categories.
First. we may have lost our opportunity by failing to impress upon him
the di gnity and high importance of our Fraternity. the beauties of Freemasonry. We have perhaps done the work in a slipshod fashion. Officers
may have mumbled the wo rds which have been poorly memorized. Those
who have been appointed to fill vacancies have had little or no advance
preparation before filling a place and our newly obligated Brother gets
little or nothing from it. He sees nothing that you and I have seen in our
travels through Masonry .... of those things which bring us back. Secondly.
man y times we insult the man's dignity. How often have we. unfortunately.
seen a m an literally ridiculed for the amusement of some of the participants
in the conferring of the degree or for the benefit of the Brethren on the
sidelines. We tell a man to kneel and pray, tell him to rise, follow his guide
and to fear no danger. only at a later date to have him treated in such a
manner that he can't see the beauties because of the lack of dignity. Once
again , perhaps we have lost the opportunity.
No man hecomcs a Mason simply by taking three degrees. any more
than a man becomes a Christian or a Jew. simply by joining a Church or

GRAND LO DGE O F CALI FO RNIA

Synago gue. It requires wo rk. It requires wo rk o n his pa rt. an<l it requires
work o n o ur part. We must impart knowledge to him and then give him
a jo b to do. Only if we improve our ritual wo rk , at t he Lodge level. and
gi ve the hcst t hat is in us . only then will we be able to improve our
me mbe rsbip and o u r Fraternity.
Brethren , we must turn the decline of o ur me mbe rship a round in order
to survive. We must all work together in order to accomplish what is best
for the entire Fraternity. We must admit our sho rtco mings. that we have
a problem and that we a re willing to do something abo ut it. Freemasonry
can and will survive in this Jurisdiction if we arc read y an<l willing to do
our share. We must remo ve stubborness and complacency. Isn't it about

It is o nly with your recognition and your help ; that is, all of us wo rking

During the fiscal year cash contributions of $85,609.50 were added to
our Pooled Income Fund . Brother Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., as Director
o f Charitable Gifts.. reports that a number of persons are seriously considering Real Property Gifts. When these properties can be liquidated. the
net asset value is placed in the Pooled Income Fund. thus resulting in a
life income for the donor or donors. This is particularly attractive to persons who have no heirs to remember or where heirs and relatives are selfsufticient. Estate tax and capital gains tax if it applies can be avoided
through making such a charitable gift. The donor or donors also get a
remainder interest tax benefit, depending upon their age or ages if husband
and wife are the donors.
It is difficult to make an accurate appraisal or estimate of assets ultimately coming to the Masonic Homes through wills. bequests or out-right
gifts. We do know from the many inquiries that our Masonic Homes are
uppermost in the minds of many of our Brethren who are preparing and
updating their wills. We are grateful for this continual expression of love
and confidence.
Brother Siems and those Brethren who have volunteered to assist him
in promoting this program are convinced that the real results are multi fold .
Because of their continued efforts in pointing out the benefits under the
several programs, we are encouraged that the Masonic Homes will continue to benefit financially.
During this past year the death of the first one of our original participants was reported. Under the terms of the agreement, the assets that this
Brother originally placed in the Pool became the assets of the Masonic
Homes .
It is important that we actively promote this program for the benefit of
our Brethren and our Masonic Homes.

representative may explain the program to a group. This method has proven
most productive, particularly whe n widows are invited to attend. At one
recent group meeting 52 widows were prese nt. Not all are interested in
the Program. and for some the Program doesn't apply. but if a few arc
he lped directly. and the others are e ncouraged to see their attorney about

and urged to become a part of this worthwhile Program.

MEETINGS
The Board of Trustees meet on a monthly basis at the Masonic Homes.
alternating between the North and the South. Meeting at the Homes provides a closer look at and better understanding of the operations of each
Home.
This is a working Board dedicated to providing the facilities. staff and
environment essential to the security and happiness of o ur elderly at Union
City and to the health. education and development of our children at
Covina.
Many hours are spent in Committee meetings on rehabilitation , long
range planning. scholarship grants. special projects. budget and finance.
Trustees and Administrators present special reports on operations of the
Homcs. resulting in a broader understanding of these complex units and
improved guidance and management of the Homes.
Represe ntatives from the Masonic Homes Endowment Board are invited to attend the monthly Board meetings. This interchange of information is invaluable in communicating our needs to the Brethren through
this important Board charged with the responsibility of raising funds for
our Homes.

UNION CITY CURRENT PROJECTS
We are in the process of rehabilitating the heating system in the ~orth
Wing, converting from steam to circulating water whereby e~ch resident
will be able to control individually the amount of he at m thclf room. At
the same time, we are having the wooden window frames, sa~hes and
screens refurbished and/or replaced as needed. This project requires temporary moves of all residents in th e North Wing and is scheduled to be
completed at the end of December.

Four apartments that were formerly used by adm1mstra_t1ve staff members will he refurbished to make them available to family members of
those residents who become critically ill and for whom it would b~ co_mforting to stay close to these loved ones. Additionally. we are contlnumg
