GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

Oh . I am not naive. I know that there are those in our Fraternity who
besmirch the very tenets of our beliefs by their bigotry and prejudices.
They haven't learned the very simple premise that where there is no freedom , there can be no Masonic Lodge. They haven't learned that where
there is bigotry th.ere can never be Freemasonry . Those concepts are incompatible.
We are all Brothers. Whether we are Christians, Moslems. or Jewswe are all Brothers, as the Great Architect of us all has made us.
This past year I had the privilege and honor of representing the Brethren
of the Scottish Rite in Southern California who received their JJrd Degree
as what is called the active candidate. As I knelt at the altar, taking the
obligations given to me by our Past Grand Master. Henry C. Clausen, who
is the Sovereign Grand Commander of the Scottish Rite Masons for the
Southern Jurisdiction of the United States, I had before me on my left .
the Five Books of Moses. the Pentateuch- in Hebrew. In front of me and
a little above rested the King James version of the Holy Bible-in English.
To my right, the Koran-in Arabic. I later learned that in other parts of
the world Holy Books of other religions would be available to the candidate at his desire. This to me was and is what the universality of Freemasonry is all about. All of these religions and mo re gathered together to
exemplify a Masonic ritual, gathered together as Brothers.
I spoke a moment ago of the great love and affection that we of the
Grand Lodge Line, and our ladies , have for each other as symboli:t.ed by
our great Grand Master and his lovely first lady. I would suppose that our
Grand Lodge Line typifies the very things to which I am referring. The
Officers of our Grand Lodge each year have formed a closeness and each
in turn calls itself "a family'' and we have learned to love each other as.
of course, men love men . We have shared joys. Regretfully. we have also
had our sorrows to share in the loss of a dear friend to us all. a dedicated
Mason and a fine man , our Grand Bible Bearer, Kermit McCullo ugh . But
let me tell you, my Brethren. in the Grand Lodge Line of California and
Hawaii this year. we have a practicing Catholic. We have Protestants of
different denominatio ns. We have men of the Jewish faith . We have m e n
whose ethnic backgrounds are English. Irish. Scottish , Swedish. German.
Armenian, Greek , Russian, Portuguese . Mexican, Korean. Spanish.
American Indian and-if you will. even an Oklahoman . You name it.
We 've got it. And I suppose you could say that's pretty nice. It shows that
Grand Lodge is really respecting each and every religion and each and
every ethnic origin. You could say it. but it would not be true. because
when Bob West appointed each of us he didn't know the religions and
backgrounds of us. And he didn' t care. Frankly. we don't talk about these
things because they're unnecessary . I had to do a little research to find out
myself. What our backgrounds are, where our families came from, what
church or synagogue o·r mosque we worship in arc completely irrelevent
to our Masonic involvement . Our Grand Master did not know. He chose
us because he thought we were the persons for the jobs; he chose us
because he felt that we were worthy of consideratio n as men and as Ma-

sons-and that"s the sole criteria. and that's the way it should be- and
that's the way it is in Freemasonry in California and Hawaii. We are Brothers. Make no mistake about that. We do practice what we preach .
Having made this pronouncem ent that we are Brothers. what is it that
makes us so? From what emanates this feeling of love? Who are Masons?
What are we?
Our Grand Master. this past year, has urged that we publicly wear our
pins . that we establish signs, clear, clean notable signs on our Mason ic
Lodge buildings and at the outskirts of our communitie s. so that the world
will know that we exist. It isn't necessary to hide our light under a bushel.
We have much to offer and we want the world to know about it. The great
newspaper supplement. of which we have heard so much , has produced
favorable comment , not only among the Masons throughout the world ,
but among those non-Maso ns whom we have desperately sought to reach ,
so that they truly may know who and what we are. But it is important not
only that we display ourselves hy pins and rings and signs . We must display
ourselves by how we act, how we affect other people. Therein lies the true
secret of our public relations story. Therein also lies the growth and stability of our Lodges.
The argument over quantity versus quality continually rages. Some say
we need large numbers . Others say. by way of rationalizati on perhaps. that
it isn't the numbers that count. but the quality. I submit to you, my Brethren. that we can have both, that we can have a large influx of members
into our Fraternity. and along with the numbers by thorough investigation
and inspection will come quality.
As Freemasons indeed we are known by the way we affect other people.
In the New MexiqJ Freemason, I read a story some months ago which I
would like to share with you. A young man was passing a pawnbroker 's
shop. The money lender was standing in front of his shop and the young
man noted he was wearing a large and beautiful Masonic emblem. After
going on a whole block. apparently lost in thought, the young man turned
back . stepped up to the pawnbroker and addressed him. " I see you're
wearing a Masonic emblem. I'm a Freemason, too. It happens that I am
desperately in need of $25.00 just now. I shall be able to repay it within
ten days. You don't know me: but I wonder whether if the fact that you're
a Mason and I' m a Maso n is sufficient to induce you to lend me the money
on my personal word? ..
The pawnbroker mentally appraised the young man. who was clean-cut.
neat and well-dressed . After a moment's thought. he agreed to make the
loan on the strength of the young man being a Freemason. And within a
few days, the young man. as promised . repaid the loan, and that seemingl y
ended the transaction.
About four months later the young man was in Lodge receiving the
Entered Apprentice Degree. He had not really been a Mason when he
borrowed the $25.00. After he had been admitted for the second section
of the Degree, he looked across the Lodge room and saw the pawnbroker
from whom he had borrowed the $25 .00. His face turned crimson and he

172

174

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

175

became nervous and jittery. He wondered whether he had been recognized
by the pawnbroker. Apparently not, so he planned at the first opportunity
to leave the Lodge room and avoid his benefactor. As soon as the Lodge
was closed, he moved quickly for the door, but the pawnbroker had recognized the young man, headed him off and, to the candidate's astonishment , approached him and greeted him with a smile and an outstretched
hand.
"Well, I see you weren't a Freemason after all when you borrowed that
money," the pawnbroker commented.
The blood rushed to the young man's face as he stammered, "No, I
wasn't. But I wish you 'd let me explain. I had always heard that Masons
were charitable and ready to aid a Brother in distress. When I passed your
shop that day, I didn't need the $25.00. I had plenty of money in my
wallet. But when I saw the Masonic emblem you were wearing, I decided
to find out whether the things I had heard about Masons were true, and
I found out that they are charitable, that they do aid their Brethren in
distress. That made such a deep impression on me that I presented my
petition to this Lodge and here I am. I trust that you will forgive me for
having lied to you."
The pawnbroker responded, "Don't let that worry you too much. I
wasn't a Mason either when I let you have the money. I had no business
wearing the Masonic emblem you saw. Another man had just borrowed
some money on it , and it was so pretty that I put it on my lapel for a few
moments. I took it off the minute you left. I sure didn' t want anyone else
borrowing money from me on the strength of being a Mason. When you
asked for that $25 .00 I remembered what I had heard about Masons, that
they were honest, upright and cared for their obligations promptly. It
seemed to me that $25.00 wouldn't be too much to lose to learn if what I
had heard about Freemasonry was true, so I loaned you the money and
you repaid it exactly as you said you would. That convinced me that what
I had heard about Masons was true, so I presented my petition to this
Lodge. Incidentally, I was the candidate just ahead of you."
And this , my Brethren , is how two men may have become members of
the Craft. What is Freemasonry? Is it the mere receiving of our degrees
that makes us Masons or is it putting the lessons we receive into practical
application-in our daily living and in our associations with our fellow
men? We can no more become Master Masons by taking degrees than we
can by picking up a baseball and automatically become a Fernando Valenzuela. Rather, the taking of the degrees puts each of us into a position,
that by earnest study and application of the truths which we are taught,
to make of ourselves, each of us, a Master Mason. And this in turn is
the appearance, the real appeara~ce we give to the world abo~t us. '
Never before have we passed through a period of greater challenge to
Masonry. It is a challenge to those who recognize Freemasonry as a force
to be used, and not merely as a forum to be served. No institution is better
equipped in this world-wide ideological conflict to build bridges of understanding between man and man without regard to race or creed. We pro-

duce men who are Masons and we must be proud of that. ln an age when
it is difficult to seek and find the truths of life. we Masons have recognized
that each man must search for that truth himself. We know that a man
can be led to the altar of Freemasonry. that he can be shown the Great
Lights, but if he refuses or makes no effort to search for the truths which
they reveal to him , he cannot hope to find harmony, inner peace and the
love of God. We cannot hope to stand as just and upright Masons unless
and until we recognize that to do so we must each first be made a Mason
in our hearts. And after we have taken the Degrees, we must live and act
as such in all our waking hours. This premise is just as true today as it was
when Freemasonry as we know it first was born. And this concept shall
never change for it is the heart and guts of our beliefs.
As a result of the tremendous progress that we have made in the technological and communications areas, the advent of nuclear energy and our
tremendous progress in the control of the physical universe with its increased speed of transportation and communication, our world has shrunk
in size until today we are living next door to peoples who yesterday almost
lived beyond the horizon of our imaginations. We are living next door to
peoples who do not understand us , and let us be frank, we do not understand them. Throughout the world we need what one Masonic writer called
"bridges of understanding" between man and man and between one people
and another. The tragedy of our progress in the control of the physical
world is that we have not made corresponding progress in our understanding of human relations. This tragedy has brought us in the nations of the
world ;.ind within our own Fraternity to a crisis. Although we are determined to be trigger ready in the defense of our freedom. we know that
this is not the ~timatc answer since someone. somewhere, may become
trigger happy and bring us all to atomic annihilation.
Our Brother General Omar Bradlev, admonished us: "Ours is a world
of nuclear gia~ts and ethical infants. We know more about war than we
know about peace, more about killing than we do about living. We have
grasped the mystery of the atom and rejected the Sermon on the Mount."
The burning issue, it seems to me, is whether the nuclear age will bless
humanity or blast it to ruin. All our progress in the control of the physical
world will indeed go for naught unless we build the bridges of understanding between man and man. unless we as Masons practice what we preach,
and there is a great deal that we preach. This is the very price of survivaL
and it is a challenge to our Masonic Brotherhood, whose universality,
based upon a belief in God, embraces-without destroying their individuality- all men without regard to their backgrounds.
We who are members of a free democracy can take comfort in the
realization that we have not been subjected to any form of thought control.
and our freedom of speech has been genuine. Because of this freedom ,
we have developed tolerance and restraint in evaluating the actions of
other people. In the atmosphere of freedom, our judgment has ever become more discerning. We must take the time to build the bridges of
understanding , we must act with reasonable deliberation in appraising our

optimism . Leadershi p ca nnot go to the half-hearte d. As Masons. we must
bequeath the vision of the un ive rsality o f o ur Brotherho od, and the courageous optimism of our spiritual inheritance. Let us remind each other
that proble ms, however serious. are but opportuni ties fo r leadership in
th e cause of humanit y. This is the requireme nt. this is the o hligatio n of
Masons the world over.
We live in a most dynamic period of the world's histo ry. If we but enjoy
the zest of living now, when significant history is being made. we will
recognile tha t many of o ur problems are but opportuni ties-oppo rtunities
for leadership in the cause of humanity. At all times. whenever the banner
of Masonry has been unfurled . it has had its ene mies. Though its pathway
down the ages has been strewn with the most fragrant Rowers of brotherly
love. relief and truth , and though the lives of the best and purest amo ng
the sons of men have really bee n magnifice nt monume nts to the gra ndeur
of its mission. yet its e ne mies have not failed to decry its merits, no r ceased
their efforts to destroy its usefulness. While the Masons of this glo rio us
century have the freedom to e rect their Temples and worship at thei r
altars. this spirit of enmity nonetheles s still exists, in adverse criticism of
o ur methods by those who arc ignorant of our mission or blind to the rich
fruitage of o ur la bors.
When we consider the antiquity of Masonry. dange rs through which •
has so safely passed , the persecutio ns of bigotry. the superstitio n and fanatisicm our o rder has so successfully met a nd repelled ; when we behold it
today wi th the glo ry of its centuries clustering about its brow. and the years
of the labo r of Freemaso nry resting so lightl y upon its unbo wed form . we
beho ld it standing upri ght and stately with all the vigors of its early youth .
its feet as e lastic to run errands of me rcy. its knees as supple to be nd in
praye r for a Brother's need. the breast as faithful to rece ive and keep a
B rother's whispered wo rd, the hands as ready and strong to support a
falling Brother. and the lips ever whispe ring words of cheer and comfort
to the ear of distress. We stand with unshod feet and uncovered head at
the mystic portals and would lay the laurel wreath of well earned fame
upon the pure white brow of that great institution which we call Freemasonry.
Freemason ry with its beautiful ritual. impressive ceremo nies and the
glory of rich centuries clustering about it. stripped of its mo ral character,
wo uld lose its greatest charm , its most precio us jewel. For mo rality is o ur
true foundation . Truth and virtue constitute the pillars of brotherly love .

We are taugh t that to be good men and true is the first and most important
lesson within o ur sacred walls . Every step of the candidate . fro m his preparation to the last sole mn scene , as he passes thro ugh the beautiful ceremonies and is inducted into our mysteries, leads along a pathway strewn
with the fragrant Rowers of truth. while diamonds of vi rtue sparkle about
its feet illuminatin g the mind with moral light , and flooding the hea rt with
the celestial goal of divine principles, while inspiring the soul and lead ing
it to a higher plane o f holy upright li ving. The trowels in our hands are
rusty from lack of use for the cement of brotherly love has not always
been spread with a generous hand . The ho urs of relief have been so destitute of service that we may well ha ve lost the gauge's use. while from
lack of labor o ur arms have become too weak to wield th e gavel in preparing the rough Ashlar for the Great Builder's use.
The mission of Free masonry in the wo rld today. as never before, is to
tight the wrong and defend the right. ls it needed? ls ou r mission ended?
I submit to you . my Brethren, that until there are no wrongs to right , no
sins to fight , no distress to he lp , no woes to heal. no lessons of purity and
righteo usness to teach, then , and no t until then, will the missio n of Freemasonry be complete. Let the prayer of every Mason's heart be that all
men were Masons and a ll Masons true men . Then . indeed. the white
winged dove of peace would hove r over all me n. Natio ns would not learn
war any more. Swords would be beaten into plowshare s and spears into
pruning hooks. Brotherly love would prevail and every moral and social
virtue would cement us. My Brethren , if we wo uld so pray, let us in Freemaso nry so live. renewing o ur allegiance to th e grand principles of Masonry and studying more earnestly her Great Light, making it the o nly

FREEMASONRY IN THE MIDDLE-EAST

We have heretofore reported on the complete "Darkness" of Masonry
in Iran as an organization and the lack of current documents of their
members residing in California. Communication has been maintained and
improved with certain officials of this Grand Lodge at time of its recess;
therefore, inquiries or requests for affiliation from those Brethren claiming
membership in a Lodge under the Grand Lodge of Iran should be forwarded to our Grand Secretary.
SPAIN

The District Grand Lodge of Spain under the National Grand Lodge of
France continues to create new Lodges in Spain, and there now exist eight
Lodges with the expectation of three being added before the end of the
year 1982 ; these are in addition to the four Military Lodges. We have been
advised that a large number of the "Candidates" for membership in these
new Lodges are former members of Lodges under the United Grand Orient of Spain. thus reducing the membership in the Constituent Lodges
under the United Grand Orient to approximately (60) sixty.
ITALY

We continue to monitor the situation in Italy which appears to be improving. justifying our action of last year. Information has recently been
received of the installation of a new Grand Secretary, Antonio De Stefano.

Many questions are asked regarding the existence of Lodges in this part
of the world, and the answer is "Yes," many Lodges do exist, but the
" Visitor" should be prudent to ascertain the "Regularity" of the Lodge he
proposes to visit, that it be Chartered by a recognized Grand Lodge, most
probably in this area of the world by England , Scotland, France, Germany
or New York .

and to Masonry in general by our Past Grand Master Most Wo rshipfu l
Kermit A. Jaco bson as a member for many year~. and retiring as Chairman
at the end of 198 1-82 of the Commission on Information for R ecognitio n
of the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North America . We are
appreciative and grateful; the benefit is to Masonry.
Respectfully submitted .

REPORT OF INSURANCE COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
At the Annual Communicatio n of Grand Lodge in October 1981 the
recommendation of the Special Committee on Insurance Study was adopted
which required our Committee to conduct a surve y to secure info rmation
of the present cost of insurance and losses sustained by the Temple Associations and the various entities of Grand Lodge: i.e., Masonic Ho m es,
our Temple , Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges.
The information so developed was to be used to establish competitive
bidding for the marketing of G ra nd Lodge and Temple Associations insurance based on the experience of losses to premiums in o rder to secure
the lowest cost.
The following data was received from 182 o ut of approximatel y 400
Temple Associations:

A limit of $1.000.000. for Public Liability insurance applied heretofore
to the Constituent Lodges, but this limit has now been increased to
$10,000,000. under the Excess Liability policy for Grand Lodge which also
covers our California Masonic Memorial Temple and Mason ic H o mes at
Union City and Covina and includes Malpractice coverage. The re will be
no additional charge to the Lodges for this increased coverage .
Insurance for the cost of reproducing valuable and important records
damaged by fire or other casualty at the Grand Lodge office was increased
to $25.000. after a survey conducted by our Grand Secretary.
Our Committee appreciates the assistance and cooperation of the G rand
Secretary and his office and the opportunity to he of service to G rand
Lodge.

180

The prospect of establishing a group or master plan for Temple Associations to secure reduced rates has been researched by our Committee
over the past three years and found legally and financially impractical as
reported at previous Annual Communications.
The replies to the questionnaire sent to the Temples indicated that at
least 100 Temples were already participating in the package plan available
through Thompkins & Company and are receiving a discount of thirty
percent or more from established rates.
The bulk of the insurance on the Masonic Homes, the Temple, Grand
Lodge and Constituent Lodges expired July l, 1982 and in accordance
with the mandate to secure competitive bidding , invitations to bid were
submitted to six separate insurance companies.
The results of their bids were reviewed with the Grand Secretary and
Grand Lodge Controller and it was determined that Travelers Insurance
Company, the current carrier, presented the lowest cost for Property, Liability, Crime and Boiler coverage and the lowest net cost for Workers
Compensation insurance based on the estimated dividend return. Accordingly, Travelers were authorized to renew the expiring coverage.
The Special Committee on Insurance Study recommended that Grand
Lodge should commence and administrate an appraisal program to assist
Temple Associations to determine adequate valuation for their properties.
Accordingly, in our letter to the Temples of March 31, 1982 we called
attention to our report "'Recommendations for Comprehensive Insurance
for Temple Associations'' dated July L 1981, advising that insurance on
their property should be based upon up-to-date valuation for replacement
cost and that careful attention should be given to verify that insurance is
maintained in line with current replacement costs and reminding them that
a serious fire loss could result in a financial calamity to the Association.
Also that the names of several appraisal companies are available upon
inquiry to our Committee.
Since the publication of our report of July 1, 1981, "'Recommendations
for Comprehensive Insurance for Temple Associations,'' o ur Committee
has been contacted by over twenty Temples requesting assistance or information for appraisals or on the premium saving of thirty percent through
the package program available with Thompkins & Company.
Several Temples indicated in their response to the questionnaire sent
them that they conside red that Liability and Workers' Compensation insurance on their Temple properties would be covered under the insurance
provided by Grand Lodge for the Constituent Lodge.
That is not correct , and it is important that each Temple Association
should carry separate Public Liability insurance in addition to fire insurance
and Workers · Compensation insurance if employees are hired for maintenance of Temple property.

Respectfully submitted.
ELMER C. GUNTHER. Chairman

REPORT OF LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT
COMMITTEE
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
This past year has been a busy and exciting one for your Committee on
Lodge Resources Development. More than 4.000 Masonic Light Award
Certificates were tabulated and sent out to members of the Craft. The
response was gratifying. An analysis of the results shed light in many areas.
Three notable observations were made:
1) It showed that few Lodges offer many programs to their members other than the long standing Grand Lodge sponsored Public
Schools and Constitution Observance programs.
2) Lodges with the greatest variety of activities also had the largest membership participation.
3) Not many activities involving the youth were reported. What
a lost opportunity!
Again this year we have seen a continuing stream of Lodge consolidations. And, again this year the reasons are the same:

1) Lodges with large membership participation in the Masonic
Light Award program also had the largest numbe r of act ivities
checked per card.
2) Lodges with active membership participation and attendance
are Lodges that involve the sideliners, not just the officers, in
planning and executing t he activities .
This is your Committee and we want to help you' We don·t ha\'C magic
potions or mystical solutions; just a tried and true approach. For exa mple,
the Family Night program has proven very successful for many Lod ges.
Unfortunately, even though this idea has been tried many times before b y
Lodges and has not been successful, it's the planning and executio n of this
activity that make it, and others. successful.
I want to take this opportunity to thank the members o f this Committee
for pitching in and helping with the tabulation of the Masonic Light Award
cards; it was a mo numental job that couldn't have been comple ted wit ho ut
their help. Also, I would like to chank Brothers Donald Souza and Leo
Mark for all of the time and energy that they have spent on behalf of the
Committee this year. A special thanks has to be given to the Gra nd Secretary, Brocher Bob Klinger, and the office staff. Without the ir help we
would not have had the certificates this year. Hats off to Brothe r Ralph
Head for the cooperative spirit he displayed in dedicating an entire iss ue
of the California Freemason to the Masonic Light Awards. THANKS FO R
ALL YOUR HELP!
Brethren, as I said at the beginning, "This is YOUR Committee; please
make use of it.

To The Most Worshipful Grand L odge. F. & A . M . of California:
The O ld Masonic H all in Los Angeles will remember 1982 as its most
popular year by visitors an d Masonic Groups since it was restored and
dedicated by Grand Lodge in 1961.
A record reservation total was chalked up with eleven Los Angeles City
and County M asonic Lodges and nine Masonic Yo uth G roups utilizing the
Temple and its historic facilities.
This increase in po pularity is due to a regular Lodge relations program
by Committee members who extolled the virtues of the Temple to Lod ges
in the community. A new tally of visitors and school children also was
recorded in the past year. Visitors to Los Angeles. seeking the site where
the City took root. visite d the Plaza de Los Angeles area where the Old
Temple is located at 416 1/2 North Main Street.
School children visiting the Temple received pencils with the no tation:
" I visited the Old Masonic Hall in Los Angeles , erected in 1854, now a
State Monument." The Committee also has a new sheet of pertinent fac ts
about the Temple that is distributed to all visitors. A highlight for 1983
will be the presentation of a Visitation Certificate to each Lodge using the
Temple for a specific degree.
The Committee has ho pes of acquiring a second permanent tena nt , and
it is hoped that negotiations will be completed by Novem ber, 1982.
The Temple is open to visitors on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and
Friday from 10:00 A .M . to 3:00 P.M . Masonic Lodges pay a rental fee of
$45.00 pe r night~ while Masonic Youth Groups pay $25.00 for a Saturday
morning degree date.
We deeply mourn the passing of Wo rshipful Brother Matthew M . Codon , a Past Master of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42, who spearheaded the
Temple restoration. He passed away in July. For more than 12 years Brother
Codon served as Chairman of the Old Maso nic Temple Committee. We
also mo urn the death of Committee member H erman Nelson.
The Temple is being kept in excellent shape. A number of the caneback chairs required repairs. We can accommodate 60 visitors in the Temple.
Brother Oliver Celaya, P.M ., is caretaker and curator. We look towa rds
another record year in 1983.
R espectfully submitted,
MORRIS C. Guss. Chairman

REPORT OF
THE QUITMAN MASONIC TEMPLE COMMITTEE
To The M ost Wo rshipful Grand L odge, F. & A . M. of California:

Upon assuming the office of Grand Master in October 1981, the Most
Worshipful Robert 0 . West re appointed the entire Grand Lodge Quitman
Temple Committee: William H. Lambert (13) Chairman ; Demar B . Dundas (13), Paul McKee (59) , John J. Glancy (101 ), and Ron ald P. Fawcett
(51 ). Lambe rt again invited Robert Richier (59) , not a Past Master, to
attend all meeti ngs as a special consultant.
The Committee had ver y few activities during the year. All of the construction work has been completed , and there was only one visitation made
to the Temple. T he re we re no big work proj ects and no important decisions
to ponder over, so uo committee meetings were held. On May 15 Nevada
Lodge No. 13, of Nevada City, California, served a buffe t lunch and conferred two First D egrees in an afte rnoon meeting. Two mem bers of the
Committee were present and took part in the ceremonies.
E arly in the year Richier and Lambert made a trip to the Temple. The
burglar alarm syste m was "soundin g off" prematurely. Richier solved the
problem quickly. On June 13 the annual Home-Coming Celebration was
held at Malakoff State Park, where the Temple is located. Q uitman Temple
was on display to the public and th ree mem bers of the Committee we re
present to tell the history of Gold Rush Masonry. There were over 2,000
visitors to the Park, and a large number of them toure d the Temple.
Prior to the visitation by Nevada Lodge on May 15, the latch mech anism
on the door of the preparation room broke. Lambert removed the e ntire
mechanism and brought it back to Nevada City. Dundas brazed the broken

197

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

part anJ reinstalled the latch while there for the Home-Coming Celebration.
One of the best accomplishmen ts of the year was having two of the
officers· jewels made. At the time Quitman Temple was dedicated. all of
the original officers· jewe ls for Quitman Lodge No. 88 were available,
except the Chaplain's and Organist's. Brother Erwin Schwarz. Senior Warden of Madison Lodge No. 23. made the two jewels, in the same pattern
as the originals. This will save borrowing these jewels from <mother Lodge
when there is a visitation degree.
The number of registered visitors to Malakoff Diggings State Park up
to August 21. for the current year. was 18,786. The Park Ranger estimated
that another 5.000 would visit the Park by the end of the tourist season.
The number of visitors making the conducted tour through Quitman Temple at this same date was 1.827, and it was estimated that another 500
would visit the Temple. This would make a total of 2,327. which is 877
more visitors than we had in 1981.
The Committee feels that Quitman Temple should get more visitations
from Lodges all over Northern California. The California State Department of Parks and Recreation considers it one of their very best historical
reproductions. Every Mason who visits the Temple seems to he deeply
impressed. It is really a "show window'· of Gold Rush Masonry. The price
of gas and the fact that the Temple is so little known seem to be the
deterring factors. When the price of gas returns to normal. the county
roads are surfaced , and the historical attractions of the Temple become
more widely known, there should he enough visitations to pay for its small
operating costs. The Committee has requested a hudget of $200 for 1983,
but o nly a small portion of this may be needed .

1981 GRAND MASTER'S RECOMMENDATION NO. 2
ADVERTISING IN MASONIC PUBLICATIONS
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Jurisprudence Committee stated that no report from their Committee was necessary as the matter is alread y before Grand Lodge.

198

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Recommendation No. 2 of the then Grand Master H. Douglas Lemons
would amend Sections 2071, 2072 and the Appendix section relating to
Commercialism whereby "other Masonic organizations as defined in the
Commercialism Regulations relating to adult orders in the Appendix'' would
allow such organizations to "advertise and solicit the general public" for
fund raising activities. Also the recommendation would allow a Lodge or
member of a Lodge the right to advertise in a medium or publicacion which
Grand Lodge recognized as Masonic.
At our last Annual Communication this Recommendation received a
majority vote but not a 5/6 affirmative vote. Therefore. it is carried over
for further discussion and vote this year.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes again this year must
urge that the Recommendation be defeated .
It is recognized thac advertising in Shrine-sponsored football games is
permitted under Section 2072 C.M.C. , but such advertising is strictly limited and regulated. Further, Section 2071 now relates only to Masomc
Youth Orders. as it should. They are separate and not controlled by Grand
Lodge. However, the Orders do have the benefit of guidance and counselling of Masons with regard to advertising.
Such would not be the case if the above Sections are amended. Allowing
solicitations of funds and avertising by Lodges and members thereof or
those organizations defined in the Appendix of the C.M.C. will create
pressures , subtle and not so subtle, upon advertisers no matter how clear
our present intent may be, and we will lose an important base of respect
for Freemasonry. We do not now make public demands for money. we arc
not a commercial venture. nor should we engage in door-to-door solicitation.
The only purpose of solicitating or accepting advertising can be to raise
money. Such activities cannot generate good will.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a '"No"
vote .

The Committee on Taxation:
The Committee on Taxation. to which Grand Master Lemons· Recommendation No. 2 and 1982 Resolution No. 15 have been referred. reports
as follows:
Normally, Masonic Lodges are not subject to federal or California i~­
come taxes. Internal Revenue Code of 1954, Section 501(c)(l0). Cahforma
Revenue & Taxation Code Section 23701(1). However, when exempt organizations , such as Masonic Lodges, compete with taxpaying businessc~,
the income from that competitive activity is taxed to remove any economic
advantage which exempt stat us might have conferred. This taxable income
is known as "unrelated business taxable income". Carry-over Recommen-

G RAN D LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

199

dation No. 2 and Resolution No. 15 would permit advertising in Masonic
periodicals. Even though advertising under these circumstances would be
directed specifically to members of Masonic organizations. they wo uld be
commercial in nature and represent an effort on behalf of the advertisers
to maximize sales to a particular segment of the public. Taxing authorities
have ruled these activities to be competitive with taxpaying periodicals
selling advertising space. Therefore the income from these activities is
unrelated business income and taxable.. See Rev. Rul. 82-139. I.R .R. 198229. 6; Treas. Reg. §l.512(a)-l(d)(l).
In computing the amount which would be subject to tax, certain deductions against gross receipts from ad vertising are permissible. Deduct ible
are commissions paid in obtaining the advertising and o th er amounts directly connected with selling the advertising. Most Lodges would not incur
such expenses. No deduction is permitted for the cost of publishing the
periodical in which the advertising appears unless the Lodge o r other publishing organization receives a significant amount of income fro m sources
other t han dues. (The exact method of computing allowable deductions.
set forth in Treas. Reg. §l.512(a)-l(f)(4)(iii) and Rev. Rul. 81-101, 19811 C. B. 352. is complicated and beyond the scope of this report.) A specific
deduction of $1,000 is also allowed. l.R.C. §512(b)(12).
The gross receipts from advertising, reduced to the extenc permissible
by the deductions discussed above, would be taxed at corporate income
tax rates. In 1983 , the effective combined federal and California rate o n
the first $25.000 of such income will be approximately 23%. For amounts
in excess of $25,000, the rate increases incrementally from approximately
23 % to approximately 51 % for net income in excess of $100,000. l.R .C.
§§5 1 l(a)(l) and 50l(c)(10). Treas. Reg. §1..511- 2(a)(l)(ii). See Generally
Rev. & T. C. §§2373 1 throu gh 23737 for comparable California provisions .
Lodges rece iving advercising income would be required to file fede ral
Form 990-T and California Form 109. Because of the requirement to file
this additional tax return , making the complicated computation of allowable deductions discussed previously, and payment of a tax at the approximate minimal rate of 23% . it seems unlikely that many Lodges will find
much be nefit in selling advertising in their publications.

The Committee on Commercialism:
Re commendation No. 2 asks the Grand Lodge to approve adve rtising
in Masonic publications .
The deletions of the various California Masonic Code Sections refe rred
to in the Recommendatio n No. 2 would clear the way for adve rtising in
Maso nic Publications provided that the provisions of Section 2070 are met.
Section 2070 provides a Lodge shall not undertake any co mmercial venture
without the Grand Master's approval.
Any Masonic publication accepting adver tising must have the Grand
Master's approval for eac h and every ad.

sell such advertising and that advertising be acceptahle. Merely asking for
advertising is a form of pressure. Our Masonic publication editors will
have the additional pressure of obtaining adve.rtisers.
Also the acceptance of advertising might cause internal disharmony over:

California Freemason Publication Board:
Since the Puhlicatio n Board of Grand Lodge consists of the Grand Master, the Grand Secretary. and the Editor of the California Freemason appointed by the Grand Master it would be inappropriate for the Board to
speak to the recommendation. I do so only in the capacity of Editor of
our official publication .
The practical and unde rstandable purpose of the recommendation is to
raise funds and in these times of inflation and increasing costs. such an
objective has pragmatic value.
I am old enough to remember when advertising in a variety of so- called
Masonic publications - some non-profit - others for profit - was permissible.
In due course of time the abuses and the pressures of solicitation led
Grand Lodge to prohibit advertising and the solicitation thereof in Masonic
related publications.
. The recommendation now under consideration carries provisio ns which
would purport to prevent the violatio ns of the past. One. for example,
requires that advertising and soliciting be conducted within the bounds of
propriety. A second suggests that fair prices be charged. and a third that
the publication be recognized hy Grand Lodge as Masonic.
As altruistic and well-meaning as these restrictions may appear, we cannot help but he concerned with the spector of censorship and a vagary of
decisions as to what is good taste and fair a nd what is ohjectionable and
over-priced .
In my opinion. the decision facing Grand Lodge is whether the monetary
gains - subject to state and federal taxes - will o utweigh the potential
problems which a re always atte ndant when judgments pertaining to propriety, good taste and value are concerned.
Not Adopted .

We agree that a limit on tenure has theoretical merit but do not believe

Bear in mind that our Grand Lodge is not a public corporation, nor are
our other Masonic entities, the Masonic Homes and the Memorial Temple.
Boards of Trustees and Committees, appointed by the Grand Master, are
entrusted with the management of these entities including the determination of compensation le:vels for them.
Salary administration is accomplished through the use of job descriptions, surveys of competitive positions outside our organization, performance reviews, and reviews of various economic indicators for appropriate
cost-of-living adjustments.
This process is carefully done with regard given to all factors which might
influence salary levels and is performed at appropriate times during the
year.
This kind of information is presently available to any member of the
Grand Lodge through the Grand Secretary.
Since this information is already available, on request, the requirement
of having the salaries of these key Officers and Administrators appear in
print in our Annual Audits and in our Budgets does not appear to serve
any useful purpose.
Your Committee on Finance therefore recommends a "No" vote.

Masonic Homes of California Board of Trustees:
As a Trustee of the Masonic Homes of California, and as the Chairman
of the Personnel Committee, I would like to present an opposing view of
the Resolution.
As we know, Masonic Homes of California is a charitable organization.
It was created by Grand Lodge to undertake and carry out its charitable
functions and is administered by a Board of Trustees selected by the Grand
Master. As such, ~t is required to establish and maintain separate but full
and complete records to account to Grand Lodge concerning its activities.
In this regard, it is the policy of the Board of Trustees to maintain an open
inspection of accounting records by any member of the Craft presenting a
reasonable need to know.
However, as a professionally-licensed public accountant it is my opinion
that an open display of sensitive payroll information does not serve a useful
purpose. On the contrary, it can be the basis for dissension and disharmony
among employers and personnel.
I recommend a "No" vote to this resolution to protect the confidentiality
of individual salaries to persons or organizations that have no positive use
for this information.
California Masonic Memorial Temple Board of Trustees:
The Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple were unanimous in opposition to this Resolution last year. We respectfully refer you
to our arguments set forth in my communication to the Grand Master at
that time. We did discuss at our last meeting the carry-over and again
opposed it.
Our opposition is directed specifically towards the fifth paragraph which
resolves that the recommendation be adopted involving the salaries and

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

benefits of the Executive Director of the Maso nic Homes, the Administrato rs and Assistant Administrators, and the Superintendent of the Memo rial Temple.
We cannot overemphasize our belief that the listing of salaries and benefits to members of Grand Lodge - of professional employees who are
not elected representatives but who by virtue of professional vocations are
functioning in professional capacities which happen to be utilized hy the
entity known as the California Grand Lodge - is totally inappropriate
and contrary to business standards and practices.
Our good Bre thre n who represent the Grand Lodge of California each
has his place in the daily commercial life. Each one is either an employer
or employee. Each must promulgate or obey normal business policies,
must be bound by them, and must carry the mantel of authority or recognize it to others. In the professional world of hospital and institutional
administration , the entire concept of salaries, budgets, and procedures of
evaluating and modifying the same is a very delicate fabric which must be
handled only with prescribed decorum. The salaries of our administrators
and their immediate assistants should not be known to each other on a
descending scale let alone to the nurses , visiting consultants , and other
miscellaneous employees.
My Board expressed a further sentiment regarding this Resolution. As
Masons we are taught to circumscribe our desires and to practice out of
the Lodge those virtues which include propriety and order. We cannot
tolerate double standards nor should we ever propose them . The members
of Grand Lodge elected their Officers. The presiding Grand Master appointed his Committees and Boards. They are all subject to normal executive and legislative recall. They in turn operating in an interwoven way,
endeavor to make the best judgments they can in that interface between
all of us as volunteer Masonic servants and those professionals who may
not be of the Craft but have offered their vocational services to our facilities as employees. We must not subject them to policies such as the publication of their contracted-for wages when we would never expect it to be
done to ourselves.
There is a specific example which involves the California Masonic Memo rial Te mple , which illustrates both of our majo r points of objection.
The salary of the Vice President and General Manage r of the Te mple is
set by the Executive Board in Executive Session , an nually. In sep arate
action but part of the basis upon which his performance is evaluated , the
Executive Vice President submits for the Board's approval the salaries of
his assistants and the various Temple employees. As a matter of Temple
Board policy, we designed and selected for use the total fringe benefit
program a nd general working condition policies that comprise the total
employment package for Temple employees. In a ll due respect to the
Brethren of the Grand Lodge , the California Masonic Memorial Temple
is a separate corporation and the legal authority and powers fall under the
total purview of the Board ; they are liable for their judgments; and perhaps the most significant point is that this private corporation known as
the California Masonic Memorial Temple draws no revenues whatsoever

for its operating expenses fro m the per capita of the members . Consequ ently, in terms of legality, propriety. good business judgment , and basic
fair play, the Grand Lodge of California should recognize the Board's
request that the individual listed salaries of the ir major employees be
confidential and on a need-to-know o nly basis.
If we have cause to object to the total performance of our Grand Lodge
or the functioning of any unit thereof, its administration , or expenses , then
o ur recourse lies in changing the committees, the Chairman and , if necessary, the Grand Lodge Officers.
We hope that our Brethren , during this 1982 Communication, will reflect
upon the justice and the propriety of our position. We have not addressed
the section referring to the Grand Secretary, for the re the parameters differ
slightly in that he is an Elected Officer of the Grand Lodge.

Th e Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
R esolutio n No. 7 proposes to accomplish two things.
First , it provides a method by which an al te rnate proponent could be

This seems proper, though the remaining proponent is authorized to
speak, withdraw, etc. We do note that the proposal does not remedy the
situation where one of the authorized proponents unexpectedly dies or is
incapacitated.
Second , the Resolution proposes that no Eme rgent Resolutio n adopted
at Grand Lodge should be effective until ratified by S/6ths of the Constituent Lodges. This proposal we believe is inconsistent with policies and
purposes of the Grand Lodge for the following reasons:
First, nowhere else is authority to ratify action of Gra nd Lodge granted
to Constituent Lodges. .
Second, the de bate which takes place at Grand Lodge and which proves ·
persuasive there cannot be duplicated in all. o r pe rhaps any. of the Constituent Lodges.
Third, Emergent Resolutio ns should cover truly emerge ncy matcers which
deserve prompt attention and effect. It is difficult to believe that the word
"emergent" was intended to mean anything but "emergency''.

too drastic remedy for any conceivable ill in our present procedure
We recommend a "No" vote.

MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE
-REMOVAL OF TRUSTEE
(12)
This Resolution proposes to establish uniformity in the removal of members of the Board of Trustees of both the California Masonic Memorial
Temple and the Masonic Homes of California. Such removal to be considered upon the request of .two-thirds of the Trustees.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A. M . of California:

WHEREAS , both the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the
Masonic Homes of California are corporate entities organized under the
laws of the State of California; and
WHEREAS, both the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the
Masonic Homes of California are classified as 501(c)(3) corporations under
the Internal Revenue Code of the United States and have similar taxexempt status; and
WHEREAS, both the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the
Masonic Homes of California vest their respective corporate powers in a
Board of Trustees; and
WHEREAS. the authority of the Grand Master relating to the removal
of Trustees of the two organizations differ in that Section 1502 of the
California Masonic Code, relative to the Memorial Temple Trustees, provides in part that "The Grand Master may remove an appointive Trustee
at any time" whereas, Section 1306 of the California Masonic Code , relative to the Masonic Homes Trustees , provides in part "The Grand Master
... may remove a Trustee at any time, upon request of two-thirds of the
Trustees, and appoint another in the place of the person so removed ;" and
WHEREAS, it is desirable that there be consistency with·respect to the
power of the Grand Master to remove a member of the Board of Trustees
of both the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the Maso nic Homes
of California.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that that portion of Section
1502 of the California Masonic Code reading, "The Grand Master mav
remove an appointive Trustee at any time " be amended to read, "Th~
Grand Master may remove a Trustee at any time, upon request of twothirds of the Trustees, and appoint another in the place of the person so
removed."

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence , to which Resolution No. 12 has been
referred . reports as follows: This Resolution proposes to establish uniformity in the removal of members of the Board of Trustees of both the
California Masonic Me morial Temple and the Masonic Homes of California, such removal to be considered upon the request of two-thirds of the
Trustees.
Your Committee finds that the language of the Resolution is sufficient
to carry out the intent of the proponents.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge. we move the adoption of
the Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 12 seeks to amend Section 1502 of the C. M. C. which
deals with the Appointment and Powers of The Trustees of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple , a non-profit California Corporation.
The proposed change would provide that, "The Grand Master may rem ove a Trustee at any time. upo n request of two-thirds of the Trustees.
a nd appoint another in the place of the person so re moved."
The present law is somewhat ambiguous as it is written, in that each
incoming Grand Master shall , in effect. appoint one-third of the Trustees
for a term o f three years each. It ·further provides. however, that "The
Grand Master may remove an appointive Trustee at any time," which, for
all intents and purposes potentially reduces the term of office to only one
year for all Trustees.
Your Policy a nd General Purposes Committee believes that the proposed
change is necessary. to preserve the integrity of the Board by removing the
possibility of undue inHue nce by any one Grand Master, thus it could
protect the Board aga inst a possible challenge from the Internal Revenue
Service, as to its tax-exempt status, by removing the issue of "One Man
Control."
The amended section would parallel Section 1306 of the C. M .C. which
governs the Masonic Homes of California, also a non-profit California
Corpo ratio n .

Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Finance.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 13 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to insure sufficient funds to
maintain the scholarship program for needy and worthy students, established by the California Masonic Foundation, by assessing an annual per
capita tax of not less than $ .20.
Your Committee finds that the language of the Resolution is sufficient
to carry out the intent of the proponents.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge , we move the adoption of
the Resolution.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No.13 seek to provide additional funds
for the scholarship program of the California Masonic Foundation by increasing the General Fund of the Foundation which would in turn generate
more income for the purposes of the program.
This they propose to do by amending Section 1704 of the C. M.C. with
the following addition:
4th : For each Master Mason borne upon its rolls as of June 30, such
per capita sum , not less than twenty cents, as the Grand Lodge shall
levy for the support of the California Masonic Foundation.
The California Masonic Foundation was created by this Grand Lodge
through funds re alized from the sale of its two Masonic Clubhouses, one
at the University of California at Berkeley. the other at U. C. L.A., in Los

223

Angeles. In addition, these funds have been supplemented over the years
from other sources, some quite sizeable.
The Trustees of the Foundation are to be commended for their management of these funds.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that the funds
of the Foundation, and the income produced the refrom, remain adequate
to support a quality and meaningful program, to the credit of this Grand
Lodge. We do not believe that the per capita assessment is needed to carry
on this great tradition. Such programs are enhanced, not by the preponderance of numbers , but, rather, by the quality of the grants and by the
care and selection of the awards.
Involuntary or mandated participation in any program tends to diminish
the spirit of charity, and so, we urge instead that every Mason in this
Jurisdiction give voluntary, thoughtful and generous consideration toward
making the California Masonic Foundation a part of his personal charitable
program.
The twenty cent assessment is rather insignificant in and by itself, but,
taken together with the collection of assessments. as will appear in the
Finance Committee Report, it then becomes part of a growing concern of
many of our Constituent Lodges.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a " No" vote.

Th e Committee on Finance:
Your Committee on Finance is deeply concerned with any addition to
the per capita tax in that it represents a mandatory increase in costs to all
Lodges. Therefore, we do not believe that the Scholarship Program of the
Masonic Foundation, however worthy, should be established as a separately designated component in the per capita tax.
The Committee on Finance recommends a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

Lodge, or to the Constituent Lodges of this Jurisdi ction. E vidence of such
benefit does not appear in this case.

condition to membership in any collateral organizatio n. It is by their own
organizational laws that such requirements a re established . Such o rganizations are gove rned by certain of our Ordinances and Regulations simply
because they themselves "purport to be Masoni c in nature." The word
" Concordant" is defined as. "Existing in concord, o r consonant ." We believe this accurately and adequately describes o ur continued association
with the York and Scottish Rite.

ELIMINATE WAITING PERIOD
(20)
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to eliminate the one year period
for membership in prerequisite organizations.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
~HEREAS, Sect. 2635 of the California Masonic Code presently requires that a Mason who has received the degrees of Freemasonry shall
not apply to any organization the prerequisite for membership wherein is
that a person be a Master Mason, until after the lapse of one year from
the date he receives the degrees of Master Mason; and
.
WHEREAS, the legislative history of this requirement as set forth in
the report of the Grand Lodge Policy and General Purposes Committee
at the 1939 Annual Com~u.nication .is that it affords an opportunity to a
new Master Mason to ga10 10format1on and become familiar with the atmosphere and spirit of his Lodge; and
WHEREAS, membership in so-called prerequisite organizations does
not and should not deter or prevent active membership in a Masonic Lodge
but, to the contrary, instill him with areas of Freemasonry more to hi~

236

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

liking and ability and thereby retain him as an active member of the Craft;
and
WHEREAS , the so-called waiting period has not proved effective in
strengthening a Masonic Lodge simply by preventing such application for
a period of one year.
NOW, THEREFO RE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2635 of the
California Masonic Code shall be amended by striking therefrom lines 8
through 10, beginning "and until" and ending "the Degree of Master Mason."
Respectfully submitted,
LAWRENCE YAPHE, PM No. 202

The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 20 has been
referred, reports as follows:
.
The proponent of this Resolution seeks to eliminate the one year penod
for membership in prerequisite organizations.
Your Committee finds that the language of the Resolution is sufficient
to carry out the intent of the proponent except that the Grand Secretary
should be instructed to change the forms of application for degrees to
conform to the legislation.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

Resolution No. 20 proposes to amend a portion of Section 2635 CMC,
by deleting the one year waiting period requirement before a Master Mason may apply for membership into any organization, the prerequisite of
membership wherein is that a person· be a Master Mason.
Adopted in 1953, this requirement has been in effect for nearly 30 years
in this Jurisdiction.
Resolution No. 20 would not amend that portion of Section 2635 CMC
requiring that a Master Mason must demonstrate his p~o?ciency in . t~e
Candidate's Lecture of the Third Degree before he may JOm prerequisite
bodies.
After nearly 30 years we should ask ourselves the question - what
benefits, if any, have been derived by the newly raised Master Mason or
the Grand Lodge of California because of the one year waiting period
requirement?
The argument that affiliation with the Scottish Rite, York Rite and Shrine
will preempt a Brother's time to devote to his Lodge is questionable. There
are far too many examples that will refute this argument. The attitude that

l

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

237

repeal of the one year waiting period would benefit only the Concordant
Bodies is simply a false assumption.
The time required to pass the mandatory Third Degree proficiency would,
in itself, prevent a newly raised Mason from immediately joining a Concordant Body.
The test of any Masonic law should be - has it accomplished the purpose intended since its adoption by Grand Lodge? It is the opinion of your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes that there are many benefits
to Freemasonry and the newly raised Master to be derived by adoption of
this Resolution.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes"
vote.

MINIMUM FEES FOR DEGREES
(21)
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the minimum fee for
the Degrees of Masonry, to adjust for the effects of inflation.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS , our Brethren in the past were wise to establish a minimum
fee for degrees; and
WHEREAS , the minimum fee for degrees has been the same since 1946
(Proceedings, p!ge 187); and
WHEREAS , the average fee for degrees charged by California Lodges
was $74.80 in 1950, $94.20 in 1970, and $98.49 in 1980 as reported in the
Grand Lodge Proceedings; and
WHEREAS , 1950 dollars could acquire four times the goods that 1980
dollars could purchase (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Indexes); and
WHEREAS , this represents a gross reduction in the value of our Masonic membership, and
WHEREAS , those Masons who represent our Membership at Grand
Lodge have a duty to provide continued leadership in sustaining the value
of Freemasonry in this Grand Jurisdiction; and
WHEREAS , the representatives at the 1978 Grand Communication believed the per capita tax to support Grand Lodge should be increased 33
per cent without a single dissenting vote.
NOW, THEREFO RE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 2684 shall be
amended by deleting the second and third sentences, "A Lodge shall not
confer the three degrees for a fee less than fifty dollars. Where Lodges
have concurrent jurisdiction, the fee for the three degrees shall be at least
seventy-five dollars, except by consent of all such Lodges." and adding in
its place, "A Lodge shall not confer the three degrees for a fee less than

238

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEED INGS OF THE

one hundred dollars from January 1, 1983 until December 31, 1986 after
which a Lodge shall not confer the three degrees for a fee less than one
hundred and fifty dollars."

W. "BILL" WASHBURN, PM
No. 207
Referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Finance.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

Your Committee on Jurisprudence, to which Resolution No. 21 has been
referred, reports as follows:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the minimum fee for
the Degrees of Masonry, to adjust for the effects of inflation. Your Committee finds that the language of the Resolution is sufficient to carry out
the intent of the proponents.
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 21 would increase the minimum fee for the degrees of
Masonry to compensate for the effects of inflation.
The effects of inflation over the past number of years have been recognized by nearly everyone.
It also should be recognized that financial circumstances may differ from
area to area, geographically, or from Lodge to Lodge. The pressures of
inflation may affect a given Lodge much more severely than even a neighboring Lodge in the same general area.
Finally, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that
it is the responsibility and right of each Constituent Lodge to establish a
level of fees and dues which will make it economically sound.
Further, it also is our belief that the Grand Lodge should not interfere
unduly with the prerogatives of its Constituent Lodges.
Therefore, we recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Finance:

The minimum fees for Degrees should be set by the respective Lodges
in accordance with their own financial needs.
Mandating future increases in minimum fees could conceivably create
hardships on some Lodges.

239

The Finance Committee recommends a "No" vote on this Resolution.
Not Adopted.

EMERGENT RESOLUTIONS
Upon consent of five-sixths of the members present, the Grand Master
declared the following resolutions emergent and subject to consideration
at this Communication:

TRANSACTION OF BUSINESS AT
OTHER THAN A STATED MEETING
(1)
This Resolution would permit the transaction of emergency business at
other than a Stated Meeting, specifically, the disposition of certain stock
holdings and reinvestment of Lodge funds within the purview of Section
2302 of the California Masonic Code as dictated by conditions arising in
the stock market, or, to take immediate advantage of investment opportunities as they may arise, the delay of which could cause loss of income
and/or purchasing power to the individual Lodge.
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, Section 2042 of the California Masonic Code (CMC) prohibits the transaction of business at any time other than at a Stated Meeting, except for circumstances as specified in that section; and
WHEREAS, Section 2308 of the CMC requires approval by the Lodge
before Lodge Trustees may buy and/or sell Lodge assets; and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS, restrictions imposed by Sections 2042 and 2308 of the CMC
have resulted in delay of action deemed expedient to the best interests of
the Lodge until the next Stated Meeting; and
WHEREAS, Lodges are already faced with a legal type delay in that
the Broker must first place the securities in "street name" before stock
certificates can be transferred, thereby adding an additional seven (7) or
more days' delay after approval has been granted to sell the stock; and
WHEREAS, types of delays such as those noted above, in an unstable
market, could result in losses of significant proportions as to reduce the
amount of funds available for reinvestment. This Resolution would afford
the individual Lodge an opportunity to expedite stock transactions versus
the present method of "having to wait until the next Stated Meeting."
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 2042 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as follows: After the words, "provided however, that" on line two, add: "emergency business affecting the
assets of the Lodge as reflected in Section 2308 of the CMC."
Section 2042 would then read as follows:

RESOLVED, that Section 2042 of the California Masonic Code be
amended as follows:
After the word "that" in line two add the following: "the disposition of
Lodge personal property investments, investment or re-investment of Lodge
funds."
To place the matter before the Grand Lodge, we move the adoption of
the Resolution.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the transaction of
emergency business affecting the assets of the Lodge, including the purchase or sale of stock holdings and other investment opportunities where
delay until the next Stated Meeting might have adverse economic consequences, by permitting action at other than a Stated Meeting.
To carry out the intent of the proponents, your Committee submits the
following legislation:

243

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:

That Resolution, determined by the Grand Lodge to be emergent business, which would permit approval at Special Meetings as well as at Stated
Meetings of "emergency business affecting the assets of the Lodge as reflected in Section 2308 of the C.M.C." gives serious cause for concern.
The proponents speak of the need for emergency authority to dispose
of "certain stock holdings and the reinvestment of Lodge funds." However,
the reference to Section 2308 assets means that property other than stock,
etc., could be dealt with at Special Meetings.
Our Code requires most business to be conducted at Stated Meetings
for good reason. Brothers expect business to be conducted at the Stated
Meeting. Only exceptions carefully noted in C.M.C. Section 2042 can be
handled otherwise. We believe this is for good reason.
Those responsible for Lodge property, whether as Trustees or otherwise,
cannot buy or sell property without prior approval of the Lodge (C.M.C.
2308). That approval must now be given only at a Stated Meeting. If this
is changed so that such business could be handled at any Special Meeting,
many Brothers otherwise concerned would not be present to grant or deny
the authority. There would be inadequate time to give proper notice of
such business to•members of the Lodge.
Perhaps a few Lodges have sufficient assets to require emergency trading
but we believe the principle of due notice to be more important than the
amount of money which might be gained or lost by such delay. We recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Finance:

Your Finance Committee makes no recommendation on the Emergent
Resolution since it has no impact on the finances of the Grand Lodge.
Not Adopted.

means for the orderly issuance of Certificates for Advancement in the
Inspector's absence. I address my remarks to C.M.C. Sections 2514, 2516,
2518 and 2520 which relate to Qualifications of Master, Senior Warden,
Junior Warden and Senior Deacon. These sections of our Code are identical except for the officers mentioned previously. Therefore I shall quote
only one - "Section 2514. Qualification of Master. Before a Master- elect
can be installed there shall be presented to the Installing Officer the certificate of the Grand Lecturer or of the Inspector of the District in which
his Lodge is situated, certifying that he has personally examined such
~aster-elect and that he is qualified to give the work and lectures entirely

of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge which relate to
the government of a Lodge." I therefore recommend that the above sections of our Code be amended to read, "the certificate of the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand Lecturer of the Division in which his Lodge is
situated or of the Inspector of the District in whiCh his Lodge is situated,".

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Lecturer proposes the C.M.C. Sections 2514, 2516, 2518 and
2520 be amended to authorize the Assistant Grand Lecturer as well as the
Grand Lecturer and Inspector to issue Certificates of Advancement.

are ample evidence that the legislative change is desirable.
We are concerned however that such recommendations as this one are
referred to Committees at the last moment, and that the Brethren of Grand
~dge are required to act on short notice. There is no express authority
m our Code for the Grand Lecturer to make recommendations but the
Code impliedly recognizes that such recommendations will be m~de.
In this case we believe the legislation should be approved and recommend a "Yes" vote.

Respectfully submitted,

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Auditing Committee, not to be confused with the Certified Public
Accountan~s whose duties are set forth at Sec. 1284 CMC, perform the
same functions as a Blue Lodge Auditing Committee performs. These
duties are set forth at Sec. 2086, Article X, Sec. 2 CMC. Past practice as
followed f~r sev~ral years required that in order for expense claims to be
processed m a timely manner a member of the Committee must share
equally with the other two Committee members in the auditing of claims.

This was done in the Grand Lodge office on a weekly basis and normally
took from two (2) to four (4) hours to accomplish.
Following the 1981 Communication of Grand Lodge we were informed
verbally by the Grand Secretary that these duties had been transferred to
the Finance Committee. However, since the procedure for handling the
work had yet to be worked out, the Auditing Committee was requested
to continue to function for the balance of 1981 until other arrangements
were completed. Accordingly we set up a schedule for 1981 as per copy
attached and carried out same.

with the Grand Lodge office staff after that date as required.

out the functions of the Committee through the balance of 1981 despite
the "lame duck" status of the Committee.

During the year research was undertaken on 6 topics for as many individuals - 1) History of the "Fraternity Club"; 2) American Library Association; 3) L. Woolans, research on family roots; 4) Tony Fels, California
rituals and Lodge histories; 5) Lois Fonesca, York and Scottish Rite jewelry; 6) Golden Gate Speranza history for an Italian Mason.
Assistance was again furnished to two University Doctoral candidates.
Miss Lynn Duminel, who has already received her Ph.D., is doing minor
re- writing of her thesis, "Brotherhood and Respectability - Freemasonry
and American Culture 1880-1930." Mr. Tony Fels has this last year assembled his materials on his thesis loosely and tentatively titled "Freemasonry's Impact on Society and Society's Impact on Freemasonry 1880-1930."
He expects to begin writing his thesis this summer.

studies compiled by this organization. The Grand Lodge of California
joined this group last year.
During the past year 61 items were donated to the Museum and several
were immediately placed on display. Noteworthy is a Masonic watch donated by Brothet Allan Cross, Lodge No. 301; officer's jewelled collar and

Bishop and officer in a number of English Masonic Bodies in the Malay
Archepelago.
During the past two years attempts were made to interest members of
the Youth Activities Committees in getting their Orders' young people
interested in disposing numerous books in our "morgue" that could not
conceivably be of any use to our Library as most were dated fiction. After
all attempts to get response from the Committee on a statewide level met
with silence, attempts were made in the Bay area; the adult response was
also discouraging. On the local level, Brother Al Buetschile of Bethel
Lodge No. 107 in San Francisco took some 850 of these books, and the
Bethel is disposing of them at rummage sales and de~lers.
In addition, the Library staff has moved 65 sets of Masonic Encyclopedias from the "morgue" to a more accessible location from where they
will be sent on permanent loan to any Lodge or Temple Library. In the
shelving thus vacated, considerable numbers of binders from the Leslie
Woodworth collection have been placed for more ready access for display.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Taxation is appointed to render advice on matters
of taxation when requested by the Grand Lodge, subordinate Lodges and
organizations under their jurisdiction. Our advice has included matters of
income taxes, property taxes, sales taxes and employment taxes. Our advice also includes the Committee's annual report which discusses items of
current interest in the taxation of fraternal organizations.
Exemption organizations, not subject to federal or state income tax,
such as Masonic Lodges, may under certain circumstances be required to
file a Federal Form 990 and either California Form 199 or 199B. Those
forms call for the Lodge to report "total gross receipts." We have historically advised Lodges to exclude Home Endowment contributions, Memorial Temple contributions or candidates' contributions which are held
by the Lodge in trust to be transmitted periodically to the Grand Lodge.
However, a Lodge was audited recently by the Internal Revenue Service
which required it to include these items in total gross receipts. While the
appropriateness of this inclusion is questionable, we would strongly recommend that all Lodges comply with this request. As discussed subsequently, the Federal Form 990 is due only if the filing entity has a certain
amount of total gross receipts for the year. There is a significant penalty
for failure to file a return if indeed one is due. If the difference between
filing and not filing a return is the amount of these contributions held in
trust, we would strongly recommend that the Lodge include them in gross
receipts and file the return to eliminate any risk of the failure to file penalty. In any event, it is important for us as Masons in our fraternal activities
to comply with regulatory requirements until changed.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

251

As mentioned previously, Lodges and certain other exempt organizations with gross receipts not in excess of a certain amount are excused
from filing Federal Form 990. This amount has been $10,000. However,
for tax years ending on or after December 31, 1982, the threshold requirement has been raised to $25,000. Therefore, with respect to a tax year
ending after 1982, the Lodge will be excused from filing Federal Form 990
if its gross receipts are not in excess of $25,000.
The Committee has also been asked to comment upon the "California
Split Roll Property Tax Initiative", which is presently being circulated for
signature. This initiative would create two different means of assessing
property taxes. Residential and agricultural property would continue to
enjoy the benefits of Proposition 13.
All other property would not. The tax rate on all other property would
be increased from 1% to 1-1/3% of property value, and there would be
no 2% a year limit on property value increases. Commercial and industrial
property would lose the protection of Proposition 13, and non-profit fraternal and social organizations, such as a Masonic Lodge, would also lose
the protection of Proposition 13. For example, if this measure is adopted
by the voters, the property taxes on our California Masonic Memorial
Temple in San Francisco alone could increase by about 920%. Similarly,
the various Masonic Temples located throughout California could be subject to tremendous property tax increases. If asked to sign a petition to
qualify this initiative for the ballot, everyone should consider its impact
upon our Fraternity before proceeding.
Respectfully submitted,
• R. STEPHEN DOAN' Chairman
WILLIAM J. MOIR
FREDERICK TILLMANNSHOFER
